04be1a0d28:995ec5e0642e6bc2.title: Survival versus Scale: The Effects of Critical Access Hospital Designation -- by Ian McCarthy, Katie Leinenbach
04be1a0d28:995ec5e0642e6bc2.summary: The Critical Access Hospital (CAH) program, established under the Balanced Budget Act of 1997, provides cost-based Medicare reimbursement to small rural hospitals in exchange for limits on inpatient capacity and service scope. We estimate the effects of CAH designation on hospital finances, capacity, and organizational outcomes using a synthetic difference-in-differences design that exploits the staggered 1999– 2002 rollout of state-level CAH availability. We find that CAH designation raises operating margins by three to four percentage points, with no change in liquidity or capital investment, as cost-based reimbursement sustains revenue while expenses fall with scale. Designation also reduces inpatient scale, with significant declines in total beds, obstetric capacity, and nursing staff. Emergency department visits also decline meaningfully, while outpatient volume is largely unchanged. At the same time, CAH designation reduces hospital closures, with no meaningful effect on mergers. These results point to a “survival versus scale” tradeoff across hospitals within a state, wherein designation-based subsidies avert closure for a small number of hospitals while inducing widespread inpatient downsizing among the many more hospitals that convert. Because converting hospitals shed more inpatient capacity than averted closures preserve, the program may reduce aggregate rural inpatient capacity even as it keeps hospitals open.

04be1a0d28:9bed03a9477f8baa.title: Indirect Variational Inference: Applications to Earnings Dynamics -- by Neele L. Balke, Stéphane Bonhomme, Thibaut Lamadon
04be1a0d28:9bed03a9477f8baa.summary: Latent-variable models are central to economics but often entail intractable integration. Variational inference (VI), widely used in machine learning, turns this integration into tractable, differentiable optimization by replacing the likelihood with a variational objective. However, guarantees of recovering the true parameters remain limited when the variational family is insufficiently flexible—a key obstacle to the adoption of VI in economics. We first evaluate VI in models of earnings dynamics and show that the choice of variational posterior is crucial. We then introduce indirect variational inference (IVI), which treats VI as an auxiliary model and corrects the bias induced by the variational approximation. IVI retains much of VI’s tractability because it does not require computing the likelihood. We apply these methods to models allowing for nonlinear persistence, non-Gaussian and serially correlated transitory shocks, and latent heterogeneity. Across simulated and empirical applications, flexible variational families combined with IVI deliver reliable estimates.

04be1a0d28:de48e358f9062980.title: When Does Randomized Oversight Align AI Agents That Can Conceal? -- by Joshua S. Gans, Richard T. Holden
04be1a0d28:de48e358f9062980.summary: Oversight changes the evidence it relies on. We ask when randomized audits and scoring align AI agents that can conceal misconduct and alter records. Stronger auditing makes undeterred violations better hidden. Because the provider writes the agent’s objective, sanctions need not stop at forfeiture, and rare audits deter every type of agent if evidence survives concealment and audit draws cannot be learned in advance. When evidence can be erased, deterrence must come from lower gains from violation, such as credit for stopping, or from costlier or fewer ways to conceal. These conditions identify what failed when agents in OpenAI’s cybersecurity evaluations compromised parts of Hugging Face’s infrastructure in July 2026.

04be1a0d28:0a7919289b23e77c.title: How Knowledge Crosses Borders: Evidence from Semiconductor Manufacturing -- by Pinelopi K. Goldberg, Réka Juhász, Giulia Lo Forte, Jeff Thurk
04be1a0d28:0a7919289b23e77c.summary: We show that cross-border learning is an important feature of modern semiconductor manufacturing and that several important channels – such as knowledge sharing along global supply chains, the movement of engineers within multinational firms, and foreign direct investment – operate through market mechanisms rather than anonymous technological spillovers. These findings have significant policy implications. When cross-border learning is mediated by purposeful economic relationships, access to frontier knowledge is neither automatic nor guaranteed. Firms and governments can facilitate - or restrict - the international diffusion of technology, implying that policies to foster domestic technological upgrading are likely to be most effective when coupled with continued access to global sources of frontier knowledge.

04be1a0d28:eae629b7dda93925.title: The Relationship between Income and Health: Evidence from Nationwide Health Exams in Korea -- by Liran Einav, Amy Finkelstein, Sehyun Hong
04be1a0d28:eae629b7dda93925.summary: We examine how physical health, health behaviors, and mortality vary with income for prime-age adults. To do so, we leverage population-wide, individual-level cardiovascular health exams linked to income tax records and subsequent mortality for a representative sample of about 350,000 Koreans aged 47--57. For both men and women, there is a negative disease-income gradient for high blood pressure, high blood glucose, and high body mass index, but not for high cholesterol. Disease-income gradients are steeper for women than men, and tend to be concentrated in the top half of the income distribution; similar patterns hold for health behavior-income gradients. Subsequent mortality-income gradients are also concentrated in the top half of the income distribution, but are steeper for men than women. Although physical health and behavior measures are highly predictive of subsequent mortality, differences in these measures by income explain very little of the income-mortality gradient, even for cardiovascular mortality. Our findings suggest that something other than differences in disease burden at prime age drives most of the income-mortality gradient at older ages.

04be1a0d28:a5e9fd3e03881cb1.title: Does Remote Work Increase Fertility? -- by Andrew C. Johnston
04be1a0d28:a5e9fd3e03881cb1.summary: Does working from home increase fertility? I study the 2020 expansion of remote work by comparing changes in births across U.S. college graduates whose majors differed in pre-pandemic teleworkability. Measuring exposure by college major avoids relying on occupations workers may have chosen in response to the expansion. Among married women, a one-standard-deviation increase in teleworkability reduced annual birth rates by 2 percent and increased full-time employment by 1.3 percent. I find no statistically significant effects on fertility among men or unmarried women, or on marriage or divorce. Accounting exercises suggest that increased employment can explain about half of the decline in births. The results suggest that returning to pre-pandemic telework levels would raise the total fertility rate by 0.09 births per woman.

04be1a0d28:a2c8d92562862bfb.title: What Can (and Cannot) Be Learned about Systemic Racial Discrimination from Randomized Controlled Trials? -- by Dania V. Francis, Rob Gillezeau, Damon Jones, Angelino Viceisza
04be1a0d28:a2c8d92562862bfb.summary: Randomized Controlled Trials (RCTs) have played a major role in detecting direct forms of racial discrimination. In this essay, we ask whether RCTs can (or cannot) play an equally important role in the case of systemic racial discrimination. We propose a conceptual model of systemic racial discrimination drawing from prior definitions of systemic racism. We then consider a range of possibilities and limitations for how RCTs can help understand systemic racial discrimination, including: (1) the feasibility of manipulating systemic racial discrimination on a large scale; (2) smaller scale approaches; (3) conducting RCTs across different structural settings; (4) the manipulation of the salience of systemic forces; (5) the role of information in reducing systemic discrimination; (6) the manipulation of the salience of racial identity; and, finally, (7) examination of strategic responses to systemic racial discrimination. In discussing limitations, we point to other approaches that may fill in the gaps left by RCTs in studying systemic racial discrimination.

04be1a0d28:69295a82f76569d1.title: Producing to Signal: Private Information in Dynamic Quantity Competition -- by Andrew Sweeting, Xuezhen Tao, Qian Wang
04be1a0d28:69295a82f76569d1.summary: We model a finite-horizon game of repeated oligopoly competition in which sellers choose quantities of a homogeneous product with linear demand and have private information about their own marginal costs, which are serially correlated over time. Focusing on fully separating equilibria, we provide conditions for existence and uniqueness. Relative to static complete- and incomplete-information benchmarks, sellers' incentives to signal low costs can substantially affect output, productive efficiency, and welfare, even when there are ten or more sellers. We apply the model to the global oil market, and compare predictions to a model where sellers can make quantity commitments.

04be1a0d28:0f724617c21725f4.title: Learning About Outgroups: The Impact of Broad Versus Deep Interactions -- by Anujit Chakraborty, Arkadev Ghosh, Matt Lowe, Gareth Nellis
04be1a0d28:0f724617c21725f4.summary: We hypothesize that broad contact, involving brief interactions with multiple outgroup members, and deep contact, meaning longer interactions with a single outgroup member, play distinct roles in shaping intergroup relations. We set up a factory in India and recruited Hindu and Muslim men to work in pairs on joint production tasks. We randomly assigned participants to work either with the same ingroup or outgroup partner daily (deep contact), a different outgroup partner each day (broad contact), or to a control group. Deep contact strengthens social and economic ties with the outgroup partner. But only broad contact reduces the majority group's misperceptions about outgroup strangers. Using within-treatment variation in partners’ pre-treatment productivity, we show that participants in both arms learn about their partners, but broad participants also generalize these belief updates to strangers. These findings align with a model in which independent sampling promotes learning about outgroups more than prolonged interaction with a single individual does. Nevertheless, neither type of contact changes behavior toward the wider outgroup.

04be1a0d28:0e6757d8b64b6554.title: Explaining Realized Returns: Roll’s R2 40 Years Later -- by Bryan T. Kelly, Yinan Su, Chao Zhang
04be1a0d28:0e6757d8b64b6554.summary: Can we explain asset price movements even with ex post observations of their drivers? Reinterpreting Roll’s (1988) AFA Presidential Address, “R2,” as a modern empirical exercise, we show that conventional macroeconomic, cash-flow, expectations, and flow variables deliver out-of-sample R2 values that are often negative and otherwise below 10% for monthly U.S. equity returns and are unavailable at the daily frequency. We use generative AI to extract newspaper-stated reasons from Wall Street Journal market summaries and filter out price and return language. These reasons explain around 30–40% of daily and monthly returns out of sample. Their content maps to interpretable themes, including corporate news, macroeconomic conditions, monetary policy, sentiment, and geopolitics.

04be1a0d28:cbc09a82a7bcdcdb.title: The Impact of Central Bank Stock Purchases: Evidence from Discontinuities in Policy Rules -- by Masao Fukui, Masayuki Yagasaki
04be1a0d28:cbc09a82a7bcdcdb.summary: We trace the impact of central bank stock purchases by exploiting discontinuities in the Bank of Japan's policy rule, which triggers purchases when stock market index movements fall below a threshold. In normal times, the purchases raise the long-term interest rate while leaving no detectable impact on stock prices. After the introduction of yield curve control, which pegs the long-term yield at 0%, interest rates stop responding and stock prices rise robustly following the purchases. Although these results are inconsistent with the inelastic market hypothesis in its original form, general equilibrium extensions with endogenous interest rates explain our findings.

04be1a0d28:778010ecf4fa15ad.title: Road Pricing under Heterogeneity -- by Itai Ater, Brad Ross, Adi Shany, Shoshana Vasserman
04be1a0d28:778010ecf4fa15ad.summary: Congestion pricing policies are widely debated and critics often argue that toll costs outweigh congestion relief. We show theoretically that welfare gains depend on two forces: the extent of driver heterogeneity—both in preferences and in exposure to highly demanded roads and times of day—and the extent of revenue recycling. We quantify the impact of both forces using data from a large-scale experiment that tracked driving behavior with and without usage-based congestion pricing incentives for nearly 10,000 drivers over two years. Using a model of time-varying traffic equilibrium with heterogeneous drivers and a granular road network, we show that a congestion pricing policy using the experiment's price schedule would raise welfare by as much as adding a new lane to every highway and would raise enough revenue to fully compensate losers. Moreover, the extent of driver heterogeneity entails that optimal prices can improve net welfare with only a small fraction of toll revenue.

04be1a0d28:f7cda0aedf33250b.title: Access to Capital and the IPO Decision: An Analysis of US Private Firms -- by Andres Almazan, Nathan Swem, Sheridan Titman, Gregory Weitzner
04be1a0d28:f7cda0aedf33250b.summary: We analyze firms’ IPO decisions using detailed financial data on US private firms. Firms with higher external capital needs are more likely to go public. Following the IPO, firms increase investment and debt issuance, leaving their leverage ratios un-changed from pre-IPO levels. Finally, newly public firms borrow from an expanded pool of lenders on improved terms, and the within-firm dispersion in banks’ private risk assessments declines. Our analysis suggests that firms go public to improve their access to capital, which is facilitated by reduced asymmetric information, and that the benefit extends beyond the IPO itself to new sources of debt.

04be1a0d28:1f89b5b0fa9e2d37.title: Industrial Policy via the IPO Market -- by Zhiguo He, Yiming Qian, Xi Sun, Wang Renxuan
04be1a0d28:1f89b5b0fa9e2d37.summary: This paper studies how China uses access to public equity markets as an instrument of industrial policy. We find that policy-favored status, rather than industry Tobin's Q, predicts IPO activity, in contrast to the United States. The effect is economically large: our estimates imply that favored industries had 287% more IPOs and 148% higher IPO proceeds than non-favored industries over 2002 to 2022. We develop a framework to interpret these findings: the government shapes the number of listing opportunities available across industries, while market forces determine which firms obtain these opportunities based on firm fundamentals. Consistent with our framework, policy favor also predicts a valuation premium which persists after listing.

04be1a0d28:048bff9412d875b4.title: Gains from Trade in Gun Policy: A Compensation-Based Benchmark -- by Bradley Shapiro, Sara Drango, Sarah Moshary
04be1a0d28:048bff9412d875b4.summary: Policies restricting gun sales face substantial political opposition and constitutional constraints. In this paper, we ask how costly it would be to induce potential hand-gun buyers to choose less lethal alternatives. Pairing stated-choice experiments with a behavioral model of firearm choice, we estimate the payments required to induce substitution away from handguns toward long guns or no gun purchase. We then compare these payments with the resulting mortality benefits. We find substantial gains from trade: many prospective handgun buyers require relatively little compensation to switch and targeted compensation can avert homicides at a social cost well below conventional estimates of the value of a statistical life. The extent to which these gains can be realized through compensation, however, depends on the state’s information about which consumers would change their choices and at what price. Without this information, uniform subsidies pay consumers who would choose an alternative anyway and overcompensate those willing to switch for less, sharply increasing government expenditure and reducing the optimal scale of compensation.

04be1a0d28:622461a5deb729f4.title: Measurement Error in Self-Reported Data on Stigmatized Behavior: Experimental Evidence on Intimate Partner Violence -- by Jorge M. Agüero, Ursula T. Aldana, Erica M. Field, Veronica Frisancho, Ignacio Rodriguez Hurtado, Javier Romero
04be1a0d28:622461a5deb729f4.summary: Error in the measurement of key development outcomes affects our understanding of socioeconomic phenomena and their policy implications. This paper focuses on measuring intimate partner violence (IPV), a public health issue affecting women globally. We introduce a novel, privacy-enhancing data collection method using a ballot, comparing it to standard survey techniques in which responses are not kept private from enumerators, and list experiments, an approach ensuring complete anonymity. Our findings show that improved privacy yields higher and more accurate IPV reports than both, especially among women with low education. By linking our data with two natural experiments, we demonstrate that the non-random nature of underreporting with standard methods can lead to biased estimates of IPV determinants.

04be1a0d28:4961d6b64d8335a9.title: Strategic Complementarity and Persistence in Linear-Quadratic Mean Field Games -- by Fernando E. Alvarez, David Argente
04be1a0d28:4961d6b64d8335a9.summary: We study the relation between strategic complementarities and aggregate persistence in linear-quadratic mean field games with interactions in states and actions. The framework provides local approximations to common macroeconomic problems, including capital accumulation and multiproduct pricing. We show that the equilibrium aggregate dynamics coincide with those of a single-agent linear-quadratic control problem in which state and action curvatures are adjusted for strategic interactions. This result gives conditions for equilibrium existence, establishes uniqueness, and links strategic interactions to aggregate adjustment. We establish conditions under which stronger state complementarities increase persistence, while stronger action complementarities reduce it, even in multidimensional problems whose underlying matrices are not simultaneously diagonalizable. Under these conditions, internalizing state complementarities makes the utilitarian planner’s allocation more persistent, while internalizing action complementarities makes it less persistent. With common shocks, we give conditions under which individual and aggregate dynamics can be combined to identify strategic interactions and model parameters. Finally, we extend the analysis to interactions through higher moments of the state distribution.

04be1a0d28:3df362fcfa7a3b2b.title: Affirmative Action in Centralized College Admissions Systems -- by Nano Barahona, Cauê Dobbin, Sebastián Otero
04be1a0d28:3df362fcfa7a3b2b.summary: We study the consequences of affirmative action in college admissions. We develop an empirical framework that distinguishes the effects on marginally benefited and displaced students from the overall effects of the policy. The overall effects include equilibrium reallocations as benefited students leave seats that others fill and displaced students take seats elsewhere, displacing others in turn. We apply this framework to a large-scale policy in Brazil that required all federal institutions to reserve half their seats for racially and socioeconomically disadvantaged applicants. Exploiting admissions cutoffs, we find that marginally benefited targeted students attend and graduate from higher-quality programs. Their graduation gains are about twice the losses of marginally displaced non-targeted students, reflecting targeted students’ weaker outside options. To evaluate the overall effects, we estimate a model of degree choices and potential outcomes. Among all reallocated students, benefited students still gain nearly twice what displaced students lose, but equilibrium reallocations make the policy displace about 30% more students than it benefits. Non-targeted students’ losses therefore offset about two-thirds of targeted students’ graduation gains, leaving a modest net gain across all students.

04be1a0d28:2396bd3766603d6c.title: Estimating the Impact of Targeted Public Policies with Limited Data -- by Kelly M. Jones, Mayra Pineda-Torres
04be1a0d28:2396bd3766603d6c.summary: Many public policies aim to support (or change the behavior of) a specific, targeted sub-group of the population. To measure the causal impacts of such policies, social scientists use quasi-experimental methods of policy evaluation, but are often hampered by data availability issues, especially regarding targeted populations, who are often disadvantaged and/or vulnerable. We use power calculations to quantify the challenge of detecting a policy’s impact on a small minority population based on population level data, using the impact of abortion bans on economic welfare as an example. We provide insight into this challenge and a roadmap for how researchers can calculate, ex-ante, whether their study is sufficiently powered to detect reasonably meaningful effect sizes.

04be1a0d28:12bbb3bf42acf706.title: Do Judges Move Markets? Ideological Shifts in the Supreme Court and Macroeconomic Expectations -- by Thomas Drechsel, Naixin Zhang
04be1a0d28:12bbb3bf42acf706.summary: This paper studies how judicial ideology shapes financial markets' expectations about the macroeconomy. We use unexpected deaths of U.S. Supreme Court Justices as quasi-experimental shifts in the Court's ideological balance. High-frequency asset price responses reveal how markets perceive the macroeconomic consequences of these ideological shifts. We find that a more conservative Court is associated with lower inflation expectations, lower real activity expectations, and lower bond yields. A shift towards a more liberal Court induces the opposite responses. The finding that inflation and activity expectations respond with the same sign suggests that markets revise their expectations about aggregate demand, rather than aggregate supply. Moreover, contrasting the yield responses with estimates from studies of fiscal policy news indicates that a more conservative (liberal) Court leads markets to expect tighter (looser) future fiscal policy. We validate our quasi-experimental setup with sectoral asset price dynamics, such as high-frequency responses of clean energy and health care stocks. Taken together, our findings are consistent with markets interpreting changes in the Supreme Court's ideological composition as news about future fiscal expansions or contractions.

04be1a0d28:63989b87beecf638.title: When Cash Flows Turn Negative: Liquidity-Driven Selling by Pension Funds -- by Aleksandar Andonov, Kristy A. E. Jansen, Joshua Rauh
04be1a0d28:63989b87beecf638.summary: Pension funds are long-horizon investors with predictable liability structures. As such, they are often perceived as investors who can provide liquidity and stabilize markets. However, pension funds increasingly face negative operating cash flows as benefit payments exceed contributions. Using aggregate data on U.S. public pension funds combined with granular holdings obtained through public records requests, we document three findings that challenge the conventional view of pension funds as stabilizing investors. First, pension funds with more negative cash flows do not adjust their target asset allocations and maintain low allocations to safe and liquid assets. Second, because of these limited safe asset buffers, pension funds meet cash flow shocks primarily by selling equities, absorbing $0.67 per dollar of shock through equity sales. At the security level, pension funds sell across equities rather than following a safe and liquid-assets-first approach. Third, pension funds sell equities even when equity returns are negative, indicating that these trades reflect liquidity needs rather than portfolio rebalancing. Together, these findings show that pension funds have become regular sellers in equity markets rather than contrarian, stabilizing investors.

04be1a0d28:49aa075a157445f5.title: Inverted Gravity -- by James E. Anderson, Mario Larch, Yoto V. Yotov
04be1a0d28:49aa075a157445f5.summary: We invert structural gravity to recover trade cost changes delivering targeted outcomes. For attainable welfare targets, one instrument per target yields a unique solution. At unchanged producer prices and to first order, each instrument must change by the welfare target divided by its own expenditure share; the required domestic change is about the size of the target, while the import change is several times larger. Inverting observed trade flows gives a separate trade cost change for each of the two directions in which a pair of countries trades. Applications to NAFTA and world trade illustrate the benefits of our approach.

04be1a0d28:ae7edc89a8124653.title: Inference for Regression with Clustered or Spatially Correlated Data I: Framework and Clustering -- by A. Colin Cameron, Douglas L. Miller
04be1a0d28:ae7edc89a8124653.summary: Many regression analyses use observations that are correlated within uncorrelated clusters and/or are correlated in distance or other spatial measure. Such data are often positively correlated. This reduces the information content of an additional observation compared to the default of independent observations. Consequently, failure to adjust standard errors for such correlation leads to confidence intervals that are too narrow, and to hypothesis tests that over reject. In this paper we first provide a general framework. We then focus on inference when observations are correlated within cluster and uncorrelated across clusters. We detail cluster-robust inference methods, particularly methods that provide improved finite-sample performance when there is not a large number of clusters. Such adjustments are often necessary. A companion paper, Cameron and Miller (2026), presents inference when correlation is spatially dampening in the distance between observations. The two papers are intended to provide a guide to empirical researchers.

04be1a0d28:dec14bf201a18996.title: Inference for Regression with Clustered or Spatially Correlated Data II: Spatial Correlation -- by A. Colin Cameron, Douglas L. Miller
04be1a0d28:dec14bf201a18996.summary: This article presents inference for regression with data that are correlated across some measure of distance; most often geographic distance. Failure to appropriately adjust standard errors can lead to confidence intervals that are too narrow, and hypothesis tests that over-reject. If spatial correlation exists within region but not across regions then one can use cluster-robust inference methods presented in the companion paper, Cameron and Miller (2026). In this paper we focus on methods when spatial correlation is dampening in distance. Then the standard inference method is the spatial HAC of Conley (1999). This method does not work well when spatial persistence is high, and alternative inference methods are needed. Additionally it is important that regression models control for any spatial trends to avoid finding spurious correlation.

04be1a0d28:c3bd7b5072cdf77b.title: Crowding Out Temptation: Experimental Evidence on Savings and Health Behaviors in Kenya -- by Harsha Thirumurthy, Elizabeth Bair, Dean Yang, Teniola Egbe, Benard Ayieko, Julius Wesonga, Sue Napierala, Connie Celum, Mary Putt, Carol S. Camlin, Mark Ayallo
04be1a0d28:c3bd7b5072cdf77b.summary: Alcohol use, transactional sex, and gambling carry significant health and economic consequences. We conducted a randomized controlled trial in Kenya to assess whether these behaviors could be altered with a savings intervention that provided lottery-based interest, goal-setting support, and savings reminders. Over 24 months, the intervention increased formal savings and assets, financed primarily by lower spending on alcohol, transactional sex, and gambling. It also reduced hazardous drinking by 26 percent and intimate partner violence by 15 percent. HIV/STI incidence declined by 8 percent, though this was not statistically significant. Savings interventions can simultaneously boost financial security and change health behavior.

04be1a0d28:6884cca977965181.title: A Framework for Integrating Climate Goals into Trade Agreements -- by Farid Farrokhi, Ahmad Lashkaripour, Homa Taheri
04be1a0d28:6884cca977965181.summary: A critical tension in global governance is that trade agreements have evolved largely in isolation from climate policy. This paper shows that the two domains generate systematic cross-externalities: larger gains from trade are associated with greater climate externalities imposed on partners, while linking carbon taxes to trade agreements produces distributive externalities that undermine the balance of trade concessions. To address this tension, we present a framework to integrate harmonized carbon pricing into the WTO subject to institutional and political-feasibility constraints. We explore two linkage designs. The first is a centralized Climate Fund, where all members apply a common demand-side carbon tax and contribute a portion of the revenues to the fund, capped by fiscal constraints. The Fund then reallocates these contributions to balance the tax burden across countries, subject to informational constraints. Quantitative analysis shows that even a simple fund allocation rule can sustain a carbon price of $138 per ton of CO2, reducing global emissions by 54%. The main binding constraint is informational: knowing the precise incidence of the carbon tax across countries ex ante would raise the feasible price to $265. The second is a decentralized design without transfers. Each member meets a carbon tax revenue floor but retains full discretion over its mix of demand-side and supply-side taxes. Energy exporters choose supply-side taxes while energy importers opt for demand-side taxes. These choices organically balance the tax burden and yield a 47% reduction in global emissions, almost rivaling the centralized Climate Fund.

04be1a0d28:14edfa994468ce78.title: Does Food Assistance Drive Spending on Sugary Foods? Evidence from the Pandemic Electronic Benefit Transfer Program -- by Georgina Cisneros, Brandyn F. Churchill
04be1a0d28:14edfa994468ce78.summary: We provide evidence on the extent to which food assistance affects spending on sugary items by studying the Pandemic Electronic Benefit Transfer (P-EBT) program, which provided funds to families of children who lost access to free and reduced-price school meals due to COVID-19 pandemic school closures. Leveraging state-level variation in the timing of P-EBT disbursements using a stacked difference-in-differences identification strategy with NielsenIQ Consumer Panel data, we find that P-EBT disbursement was associated with a 16-percent increase in weekly spending on sugary items among SNAP-eligible households with school-aged children. Notably, this increase exceeded the percentage increase in overall food spending for this group, suggesting that SNAP-eligible households with school-aged children allocated a disproportionately large share of their P-EBT-driven purchases toward sugary items relative to their pre-period baseline. We do not detect changes among households unlikely to have received P-EBT benefits or in placebo disbursement years.

04be1a0d28:bd0bfed2bf815fca.title: Consumption, Savings, and Earnings Responses to Financial Windfalls -- by Rajashri Chakrabarti, Philippe d'Astous, Kory Kroft, Sheisha Kulkarni, Vyacheslav Mikhed, Matthew J. Notowidigdo, Sahil Raina, Barry Scholnick
04be1a0d28:bd0bfed2bf815fca.summary: We estimate the causal effects of a financial windfall on consumption, savings, and wage earnings using linked administrative data on a large sample of Canadian lottery winners. Using separate linkages of lottery winners to income tax records and credit bureau data, we estimate how lottery winnings affect consumption measured through credit card spending, savings through financial asset accumulation and debt repayment, and wage earnings from tax records. We then examine how these responses vary across the income distribution. We find that high-income individuals allocated a larger share of lottery winnings to savings and leisure, while low-income individuals spent a larger share on consumption. We illustrate the policy relevance of these heterogeneous responses through three applications: designing fiscal stimulus programs, evaluating a Universal Basic Income (UBI), and determining optimal top tax rates on wage earnings and savings.

04be1a0d28:3ef9113d315e5c2f.title: Approximating the Equilibrium Effects of Informed School Choice -- by Claudia Allende, Francisco Gallego, Christopher Neilson
04be1a0d28:3ef9113d315e5c2f.summary: We study how information about school quality affects families’ choices and how scaling up the intervention changes its impact. In a randomized trial in Chile, we offer families a short video and a personalized school report card before they enroll their children. Treated families choose schools with higher test scores and value added. Among families reached before enrollment, treated children score about 0.2 standard deviations higher in fourth grade, with positive but less precise estimates on later assessments. We embed the experimentally identified demand shift in a structural model of school choice and competition to study equilibrium effects at scale. Capacity constraints and centralized assignment attenuate the demand-side gains, but the same shift in demand strengthens schools’ incentives to improve quality, and the supply response roughly offsets the congestion effect. More generally, equilibrium scaling can alter experimental effects in either direction because congestion and endogenous quality responses work against each other. We use the model to guide the design of a follow-up cluster-randomized experiment, focusing on the tradeoff between precision and contamination from equilibrium spillovers.

04be1a0d28:46e404865d12b6cd.title: When Does Bad News Stick? Topic-Level Asymmetry in Narrative Dynamics -- by Isha Agarwal, Wentong Chen, Eswar S. Prasad
04be1a0d28:46e404865d12b6cd.summary: When does bad news stick? This paper shows that the persistence of media sentiment depends not only on whether news is good or bad, but also on what the news is about. Using the complete Wall Street Journal archive from 1990 to 2025, we construct monthly positive and negative sentiment indices for twelve economic topics and estimate topic-specific sentiment dynamics. Bad-news innovations generate larger cumulative responses than positive-sentiment innovations in every topic, indicating that negativity asymmetry is a broad feature of media sentiment. But the size of this asymmetry varies sharply across topics. The bad-minus-positive persistence gap is largest in security and human rights, firms and corporate strategy, health and public safety, and real estate and financial stability. Bad-news persistence is also sizable in data-rich topics such as financial markets, real estate, and corporate news, suggesting that frequent information arrival does not necessarily lead narratives to revert quickly. These findings show that aggregate sentiment indices mask substantial topic-level heterogeneity in the asymmetric dynamics of narratives, with potential implications for how persistent negative sentiment shapes expectations, asset prices, and real economic outcomes.

04be1a0d28:91b3186eb2ec2660.title: Large Language Models as Voting Mechanisms -- by Raša Karapandža, Yaw Nyarko
04be1a0d28:91b3186eb2ec2660.summary: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly provide economic and financial advice. We develop a microeconomic framework for understanding this role. We prove that an LLM acts like a voting rule: each input text is an election, possible continuations are candidates, and output probabilities are vote shares derived from the training corpus. Such rules can generate Condorcet cycles, implying intransitive pairwise recommendations and potential money-pump exploitation. Using ChatGPT-4o, we identify millions of cycles in pairwise investment choices among S&P 100 firms. Our theorems establish the voting interpretation on the training data and support its use off-sample. We also show that correcting cycles ex post is generally infeasible. Finally, temperature changes the voting rule: at T = 1, outputs are sampled in proportion to vote shares; lower temperatures favor the plurality winner, whereas higher temperatures flatten probabilities toward uniformity.

04be1a0d28:b7a0dec58ae35462.title: Asymmetric Reversals -- by Federico Baldi-Lanfranchi, Pierre Collin-Dufresne, Kent D. Daniel
04be1a0d28:b7a0dec58ae35462.summary: Short-term return reversal is one of the most robust asset-pricing anomalies, and is commonly linked to liquidity provision. We decompose individual firm stock returns into two distinct components: SYS, the component of returns that can be linked to systematic risk and public information releases; and an orthogonal residual RES. The RES component reverses, while the SYS component exhibits continuation. Moreover, the residual reversals are highly asymmetric: positive residual shocks reverse much more slowly than negative shocks. A return factor based on asymmetric idiosyncratic reversal subsumes the idiosyncratic volatility factor and a broad set of other short-horizon anomalies. Our findings suggest that asymmetric idiosyncratic reversal (AIR) is the primary driver of short-term return predictability.

04be1a0d28:832bf5df3e1a3181.title: Soft Reserves, Learning and Bid Adjustment in Advertising Auctions -- by Joshua S. Gans
04be1a0d28:832bf5df3e1a3181.summary: An advertiser in a second-price auction sees what it paid, not the rival bids that supposedly set the price. Akbarpour and Li (2020) show that an auctioneer can therefore charge a winner up to its bid undetected. The Federal Trade Commission alleges that Amazon’s advertising auctions, described as second-price, used soft reserves that did this. We ask whether repeated bidding exposes such charges and what adjustment does to welfare. If each charge equal to the bid is flagged, the soft reserve is exposed quickly, however much the advertiser trusted the description. If reports show only win rates and expected charges, it is indistinguishable from a second-price auction at any fixed bid: an advertiser that trusts the description and bids its value never learns, and one that doubts it but bids for current profit needs a number of auctions at least inversely proportional to its doubt before it considers a soft reserve more likely than not. The second-price description and aggregate reporting are complements. Among informed, symmetric advertisers, the soft reserve raises no more revenue than a second-price auction, and when only some advertisers adjust, placements are misallocated. Disclosure returns surplus to advertisers; removing the surcharge also restores efficiency.

04be1a0d28:5508623319a71579.title: Schooling and Political Activism in the Early Civil Rights Era -- by Daniel Aaronson, Mark Borgschulte, Sunny Liu, Bhashkar Mazumder
04be1a0d28:5508623319a71579.summary: Does education lead to political activity? We find that a large, early 20th century school construction program, the Rosenwald schools, led to more NAACP branches in the rural South starting in the early 1940s, i.e. prior to the classic U.S. Civil Rights Movement. Branch growth was stronger where Jim Crow occupational segregation prevented Black men from realizing some of the economic gains of their education. Our findings lend support to theories emphasizing that economic context can act as a critical mediator in determining whether human capital causes political engagement.

04be1a0d28:b0f12c0f51a07471.title: Welfare Analysis with Complementarities: When Direct and Total Responses Are Sufficient -- by David Argente
04be1a0d28:b0f12c0f51a07471.summary: Complementarities can have important welfare consequences, but quantifying these effects would seem to require identifying and valuing the underlying mechanisms separately. This paper shows that this need not be the case. I provide necessary and sufficient conditions under which baseline subsidized activity and the direct and total responses to a subsidy determine aggregate willingness to pay. A sufficient condition for valuing the equilibrium adjustment is that it has the same effect on utility as an additional subsidy common to all agents and relevant actions. The formula is easy to apply to existing estimates and guides the design of new experiments.

04be1a0d28:b9bc62437b7e878c.title: Aging Out of Coverage: Lessons from the West Virginia $1,000 Adult Dental Benefit -- by Daniel S. Grossman, Kole T. Reddig, Jane Ruseski, Fotinos Panagakos
04be1a0d28:b9bc62437b7e878c.summary: This paper studies the utilization of dental services during the recent implementation of an adult (age 21 and over) Medicaid dental benefit in West Virginia. We analyze claims data and find: 1) before implementation, quarterly utilization of preventative and restorative services falls from 8% at age 20 to virtually 0% at age 21; 2) post-implementation, utilization falls from 8% at age 20 to 5% at age 21, implying a net increase of 50% of baseline utilization; 3) the net effect of the dental benefit is significantly larger in counties with a larger number of oral health care provider practices. Our results provide evidence that public health insurance expansions are dampened in markets with a limited supply of provider practices.

04be1a0d28:e41fa36edabf01d6.title: Limits to Arbitrage and Prediction Market Efficiency: the Case of PredictIt -- by Eric Zitzewitz
04be1a0d28:e41fa36edabf01d6.summary: PredictIt is a CFTC-regulated US prediction market focused on political outcomes. It was very successful in attracting participants in the 2016-22 period, running liquid markets on topics predecessors had tried unsuccesfully. During this period, investors were limited to $850 positions in each contract, which limited arbitrage trading. PredictIt exhibited much larger pricing biases than previously studied prediction markets. Bid prices often persistently added to more than 110, implying an immediate arbitrage profit even after fees. Prices exhibited an overpricing of longshots that was larger than in other prediction markets. The experience of PredictIt suggests that limiting stakes may undermine the ability of prediction markets to accurately price event probabilities.

04be1a0d28:2f58e513cbb0f28f.title: Are Prediction Markets Politically Biased? -- by Eric Zitzewitz
04be1a0d28:2f58e513cbb0f28f.summary: As prediction markets become more prominent, there are concerns that they will be a conduit for political bias. I analyze prediction markets returns from 1880 to 2025 and find no evidence of an overpricing of either left or right-leaning candidates, across a variety of subsamples. In recent elections, there is also no overpricing of either male or female, white or non-white, or young or old candidates. Most political prediction markets exhibit a favorite-longshot bias, and markets on near-term polling averages exhibit a very small overpricing of left-leaning outcomes (e.g., President Trump’s approval falling), which is detectable only because the sample size is large. For elections, however, despite attracting participants who may not be representative of the voting population, prediction markets yield predictions without systematic bias.

04be1a0d28:fe0fd28f11ec6f24.title: Targeted Acceleration in Middle School Math: Impacts on College Entry, Degree Completion, and STEM -- by David Card, Laura Giuliano
04be1a0d28:fe0fd28f11ec6f24.summary: We study an accelerated 3-year math curriculum offered in the middle schools of a large urban district that enables students to finish Algebra I and Geometry before high school. Entry to the program is based on 5th-grade math test scores, with a cutoff at the 80th percentile. Continuing eligibility requires at least a B grade in the previous year; successful completion of all three years is highly correlated with an index of non-cognitive skills. Following students for 6 years after high school graduation, we find that the impacts of admission vary widely by non-cognitive skill and gender. Marginally eligible boys with high non-cognitive skills have a 33 percentage point (ppt.) increase in the probability of completing calculus by 11th grade and a 12 ppt. increase in the probability of completing a major in STEM or business within 6 years; boys with lower noncognitive skills take more advanced math classes in high school but have no significant effects on their college outcomes. Like their male peers, marginally eligible girls with high non-cognitive skills are more likely to complete calculus by 11th grade (+17 ppt.). Their rate of graduating with a STEM or business major is unaffected, but they switch from social sciences to the core STEM majors (science, engineering and math). Girls in the two lower terciles of non-cognitive skill are also strongly affected by entry to the program, with higher participation in advanced math classes in high school, higher rates of entry to selective 4-year colleges, and higher rates of completing a STEM or business major (+12 ppt).

04be1a0d28:095bdbb76ffdb77a.title: The Regulatory Burden of Licensure Sales Laws: New Evidence on Race and the U.S. Tobacco Market -- by Dhaval M. Dave, Jooyoung Kim, Joseph J. Sabia
04be1a0d28:095bdbb76ffdb77a.summary: Licensure sales requirements are commonly justified as consumer protection regulations intended to improve seller compliance and reduce harm associated with risky products. However, licensure effects may differ across communities with heterogeneous enforcement intensity and seller responses. We study this question in the context of e-cigarette retail licensure laws (ERLLs), a policy intended to regulate access to e-cigarettes among youth. We find that state ERLLs with strong penalties for non-compliance reduce nicotine vaping among Black youths by 2.5-4.0 percentage points but have no effect on White youths. This racially disparate finding is driven by heterogeneous supply-side responses to increased regulatory burden. Vendors in Black neighborhoods are more likely to be targeted for inspections than those in White neighborhoods despite having lower pre-treatment rates of infractions. Moreover, vendors in Black neighborhoods are also less likely to sell e-cigarettes following ERLL adoption, consistent with a racially disparate regulatory burden. Together, our results suggest important distributional consequences of licensure requirements.

04be1a0d28:4be705e8da97944b.title: Avoiding Regulation: Evidence from Nursing Homes -- by Alden Cheng, Riley League
04be1a0d28:4be705e8da97944b.summary: We study strategic responses by firms to threshold-based regulations. We document extensive bunching in response to additional staffing requirements for California nursing homes with at least 100 beds. To estimate the regulation’s effect on staffing, we develop a novel treatment effects estimator for threshold-based regulations under precise manipulation, by decomposing firms into response types based on counterfactual and realized staffing and size, separating causal effects from selection. We estimate that higher staffing above the threshold is nearly entirely due to selection, with low-staffing facilities manipulating their size to avoid the regulation. These size distortions limit access, particularly for disadvantaged patients.

04be1a0d28:670e8fe9993b1a0c.title: Debt Sustainability and the Range of Multiple Equilibria -- by Olivier J. Blanchard, Pedro Martinez-Bruera, Gonzalo Huertas
04be1a0d28:670e8fe9993b1a0c.summary: We characterize the size of the range of multiple equilibria in sovereign debt markets. We show that the nature of the equilibrium depends crucially on the degree of uncertainty, which we formalize first as uncertainty about primary balances and later as uncertainty about the fiscal feedback rule. For low uncertainty, the range can be large, but it becomes smaller as uncertainty becomes larger. If uncertainty is large enough, the multiplicity disappears: the interest rate is unique and becomes a continuous function of the debt level. The source of these results is that larger uncertainty decreases the effect of the perceived probability of default on the actual probability of default, thus reducing and eventually eliminating the scope for multiplicity. Interpreting the source of an increase in the interest rate in actual situations is difficult, and complicates the use of intervention by central banks.

04be1a0d28:a0906ec82fc74258.title: Latent Human Capital: How Early Investments in Parents Buffer Against Future Schooling Shocks -- by Shruti Jha, John A. List, Rebecca C. Royer, Anya Samek
04be1a0d28:a0906ec82fc74258.summary: Do early investments in parents pay off even when treatment effects for children appear to fade out quickly? We answer this question by leveraging a field experiment in which households with 3-5 year-old children were randomized into a parenting program, a preschool, or a control group, combined with a natural experiment (Covid-19 school closures) that occurred ten years later. Prior to the closures, treatment effects on academic achievement had faded to zero across all groups. Yet, with Covid-19 school closures, effects of the parenting program re-emerge: test scores in control and preschool groups drop by roughly 0.25-0.30 SD, whereas scores in the parenting group drop by only 0.11 SD (difference: p = 0.01). Our findings suggest that parenting programs can generate latent human capital that only becomes visible when complementary school inputs are removed. This result is consonant with parental and school investments acting as substitutes in skill production. Because this latent parental capacity pays off precisely when school inputs fail, standard measurement tools for early childhood programs can miss crucial state-contingent value.

04be1a0d28:ec092453134355d3.title: Living in a Ghost Town: The Geography of Depopulation and Aging -- by Elisa Giannone, Yuhei Miyauchi, Nuno Paixao, Xinle Pang, Yuta Suzuki
04be1a0d28:ec092453134355d3.summary: How do depopulation and population aging evolve differently across regions within a country, and what are their implications for aggregate economic activity and regional inequality? Using spatially disaggregated data from Japan over the past several decades, we show that rural areas have experienced significantly faster depopulation and aging than urban areas, driven by low fertility and sustained out-migration of young cohorts. Regions undergoing these trends face declining local amenities and rising per-capita public service costs. To study the future evolution and economic consequences of these dynamics, we develop and calibrate a dynamic life-cycle spatial general equilibrium model. The model predicts widening geographic disparities in depopulation, aging, and economic activity in the coming centuries. While subsidies to declining regions can lower regional inequality, they come at the cost of lower aggregate efficiency and higher public service expenditures.

04be1a0d28:a39a7216e62bdfc9.title: Randomized to Opportunity: Measuring Place Effects for Refugee Children -- by N. Meltem Daysal, Joseph J. Doyle Jr., Naeim S. Samandari, Emil A. L. Simonsen, Mircea Trandafir
04be1a0d28:a39a7216e62bdfc9.summary: Area-level measures of economic opportunity are increasingly used to guide place-based policies. We study whether these measures predict long-run outcomes for a vulnerable population: over 12,000 refugee children quasi-randomly assigned to municipalities under Denmark's 1986–1998 dispersal policy. We focus on predetermined measures of opportunity available when children arrive and validate them using a mover-exposure design among permanent residents. Moving from a low- to a high-opportunity area (a two-standard-deviation increase) raises adult income rank by 3 percentile points (7.5 percent) and employment by 4 percentage points. It also reduces criminal convictions by 14 percent and teen parenthood by 19 percent, with more modest effects on educational attainment. Economic opportunity predicts crime and teen parenthood more strongly than other area characteristics, including local crime rates. For adult income, area-level inequality is a particularly strong predictor. These findings suggest that social mobility in the areas where refugee children grow up meaningfully shapes their long-term wellbeing.

04be1a0d28:39acb50eac0af221.title: Taxing Entrepreneurial Wealth: Evidence from Norway, 2021–2025 -- by Marius A. K. Ring
04be1a0d28:39acb50eac0af221.summary: Whether imposing higher taxes on business owners adversely affects business activity by constraining investment and inducing capitalist flight is a central question in the ongoing debate on how to tax the ultra wealthy. To shed new light, I exploit a series of related Norwegian reforms during 2021–2024 that increased dividend tax rates, removed migration-related capital gains tax loopholes, and nearly doubled the effective marginal tax rate on business wealth. These reforms spurred international debate and, allegedly, an “exodus” of Norwegian billionaires (Financial Times, 2023). While I document clear effects on migration, these responses are concentrated among the top 0.1% of the wealth distribution and mostly confined to 2022 and 2023. My results indicate that at most 100 individuals left due to the reforms. I find no evidence of significant outmigration or reduced inflows of startup founders or inventors. I estimate that absent any outmigration, wealth tax revenues would have increased by 75% from 2021 to 2024. Reform-driven outmigration lowers the revenue gain to 71.5%. My findings further show that outmigrating owners’ firms remain economically active and do not reduce investment. In a broader set of analyses, I examine whether business outcomes are affected, regardless of whether owners outmigrate, since firms may reduce investment both due to liquidity constraints or distortions to owners’ savings decisions. I compare firms owned by Norwegian individuals subject to the wealth tax with firms owned by foreigners and other tax-exempt entities. By merging historical ownership data from Orbis with the Norwegian shareholder register, I perform these analyses on both Norwegian and foreign-domiciled firms. Across settings, I find no evidence that Norwegian-owned firms pay out more dividends or invest less after the reforms, nor is there any evidence that the reform induced more bankruptcies. These findings indicate that the short-run economic costs of wealth…

04be1a0d28:5992f511de61b327.title: Physicians' Occupational Licensing and the Quantity-Quality Trade-off -- by Juan Pablo Atal, Tomás Larroucau, Pablo Muñoz, Cristóbal Otero
04be1a0d28:5992f511de61b327.summary: Occupational licensing is a widespread quality regulation that potentially increases the quality of labor but reduces its quantity. We provide a theoretical framework to empirically quantify this trade-off in public hospitals, where both clinical quality and physician shortages are critical concerns. Using quasi-exogenous variation driven by a recent and unprecedented migration of physicians to Chile, together with growth in domestic medical schools, we show that more physicians improve patient outcomes, while lower-quality physicians—as measured by licensing exam performance—worsen them. Incorporating these findings into our theoretical framework, we evaluate the implications of locally changing the stringency of the licensing policy.

04be1a0d28:c8f0d1ec78cbe42e.title: Which Workers Left the Labor Force Post-COVID Recession and Why?: Filing, Tax Credit Take-Up, and Labor Force Engagement by Occupation -- by Andrew C. Barr, Laura Kawano, Bruce Sacerdote, Michael Stevens
04be1a0d28:c8f0d1ec78cbe42e.summary: The COVID-19 pandemic caused a sharp initial rise in unemployment, followed by an unexpectedly tight labor market. Using a panel of tax data containing newly assembled information on worker occupation, we document persistent labor force exit, especially among low-income and low-skill workers. Low-skilled unmarried men are by far the most likely to exit, reinforcing recent concerns regarding the economic and social engagement of this group. Contrary to prevailing theories, we find little evidence that school closures, virus exposure, stimulus payments, or unemployment benefits explain these exits. Nor is the exit explained by additional upgrading of occupations or firm quality. Individuals who leave the labor force do not (on average) make up the missing income; however, self-employment income replaces roughly a quarter of the lost W-2 income. The facts suggest that the willingness to work for low pay decreased and preferences for leisure and job flexibility increased among a large set of workers who have found ways to get by with less income. These results have implications for tax policy, fiscal projections, and labor market dynamics in the post-pandemic economy.

04be1a0d28:d88370b15ed96172.title: Capital-Skill Complementarity Beyond Firm Boundaries -- by Gert Bijnens, Anders Humlum, Stijn Vanormelingen
04be1a0d28:d88370b15ed96172.summary: New machinery has long been argued to raise the relative demand for skilled labor, yet firm-level evidence finds no such shift at investing firms. We resolve this puzzle by looking beyond firm boundaries. Linking Belgian data on capital investments, buyer–supplier transactions, and worker skills, we show that the skill bias of new machinery arises entirely at external suppliers. Following machinery investment spikes, purchases from suppliers raise firms’ total demand for high-STEM workers by 45%, three times the rise for other skill groups, while in-house hiring raises it by less than 5%, evenly across skill groups. This external demand comes first from machine integrators and later from complementary services such as software, and is stronger for smaller firms, lumpier investments, and rapidly advancing capital, consistent with fixed and adjustment costs of hiring high-STEM workers in-house. In a general-equilibrium model estimated on our event studies, the rise in machinery per worker from 2003 to 2021 raises relative demand for high-STEM workers by 8.8 log points and their wage premium by 3.1. Measured on payrolls alone, both would fall.

04be1a0d28:86be09af4b5e060c.title: Stressful Exposure from the 2004 Indian Ocean Tsunami Drives Long-term Changes in Thyroid Hormone Physiology -- by Ralph I. Lawton, Duncan Thomas, Elizabeth Frankenberg, Cecep Sumantri, Teresa Seeman, Eileen Crimmins, Daniel Hochbaum
04be1a0d28:86be09af4b5e060c.summary: Stressful events are associated with long-term adverse health impacts, but the causal mechanisms linking exposures to disease remain poorly understood. One mechanism is persistent changes to hormonal signaling that regulate metabolic homeostasis. We examine the long-term impacts of stress associated with exposure to the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami on levels of free triiodothyronine (FT3), a circulating measure of biologically active thyroid hormone, using data from the Study of Tsunami Aftermath and Recovery. Biomarkers are measured 20 years post-tsunami in a population-representative sample age 35y+ in 2024 who, at the time of the tsunami, were living along the coast of Aceh, Indonesia, the area hardest-hit by the tsunami. Because respondents were first interviewed before the tsunami and subsequently tracked regardless of migration, the sample avoids selection bias common in long-term disaster studies. We identify the causal effect of tsunami exposure using variation in community-level tsunami mortality, comparing communities within the same sub-district. We find that greater tsunami exposure reduced levels of FT3 20 years later. Exposure also altered relationships between FT3, body composition, and cortisol and increased cardiometabolic risk. These findings identify persistent alteration of thyroid hormone physiology as a potential pathway linking severe stressful exposures to long-term cardiometabolic disease risk.

04be1a0d28:7158f2acb38e1c69.title: How Heavily Are PhD Students Offloading Their Scientific Writing to AI? Evidence from US STEM PhD Dissertations -- by Daniel P. Gross, Dror Shvadron, Hansen Zhang
04be1a0d28:7158f2acb38e1c69.summary: Large language models are diffusing rapidly into science, raising concerns that delegating research writing to AI may undermine the development of expertise that scientific training is supposed to build. We measure AI-generated writing in the dissertations of a near-census of US STEM PhD graduates from 2019 to 2026 and link graduates to their subsequent employment. AI writing is absent before 2023, present in 29% of dissertations filed in 2026, and rapidly growing. Use is more common among students from non-English-speaking countries and at lower-ranked programs. Among graduates in the same program and cohort, those whose dissertations contain AI writing are less likely to enter academic research careers and more likely to enter non-tenure-track roles or industry, with this pattern strongest among US-origin students. At the same time as AI may increase research productivity, it thus appears to also be displacing a potentially important portion of the work through which scientific expertise is developed.

04be1a0d28:5301dd9f7ee593ef.title: Communicating Performance: Textual and Financial Disclosures in Private Equity -- by Josh Lerner, Fiona Paine, Antoinette Schoar
04be1a0d28:5301dd9f7ee593ef.summary: Private capital fund managers appear to possess significant information about the relative quality of their portfolio firms even within the first three years after the investment. But the way this information is disclosed to investors changes dynamically: Textual discussions of portfolio companies have substantial information about the firms’ ultimate performance in the early stages of investment, while interim valuations are less important. Over time, this pattern reverses, with interim valuations becoming more important in explaining future returns, especially after portfolio companies have a financing event. The results vary not only with the tone but also with the content of fund manager disclosures. In an opaque market with substantial information asymmetries, textual discussions seem to serve as a signal about general partner quality.

04be1a0d28:73f809c2e19fcc6d.title: Labor Supply and Wages over the Life Cycle: Human Capital and Disability Benefits -- by Richard Blundell, Monica Costa-Dias, Graham Mazeine, Costas Meghir, Tom Waters
04be1a0d28:73f809c2e19fcc6d.summary: Work experience has been found to be a key determinant of work and wages for educated women, but it seems to play a smaller role for the less educated. For them, welfare, tax credits and family composition matter more, and increasingly so does participation in disability programmes. Here we document how labor supply, wages, health, and disability claims have evolved in the UK over the last three decades, and examine how reforms to tax credits, disability benefits and other welfare programs have changed work incentives over this period. We then introduce these features into an empirical dynamic structural model of life-cycle labor supply, human capital and disability benefit application, in which human capital combines health capital, experience accumulated in work, and education. Estimating the model on a panel of working-age women in the UK, we examine the interactions between experience capital and health capital in driving life-cycle earnings across different education groups. Our results highlight the importance of interactions in the disability benefit, welfare and tax-credit systems for understanding the life cycle pattern of hours, employment, earnings, and disability claims, and for evaluating policy counterfactuals.

04be1a0d28:66c659e719a654b7.title: The Geopolitical Trap: How Great Power Rivalry Protects Rising Powers -- by Johann Caro-Burnett, Sebastian Galiani, Gustavo Torrens
04be1a0d28:66c659e719a654b7.summary: Why do rising powers survive periods in which established states can still suppress them? Existing theories of preventive war emphasize commitment problems between declining and rising states, which can make adverse power shifts especially dangerous. We show that commitment problems among established rivals can have the opposite effect. Preventive action against a rising power can alter the incumbent’s relationship with another state. Under opportunistic rivalry, prevention temporarily exposes the incumbent to exploitation by an existing rival. Under defensive rivalry, successful prevention strengthens the incumbent by eliminating a potential counterweight, giving its rival an incentive to protect the rising state. In both cases, third-party responses can deter preventive action that would occur in an otherwise identical dyadic setting. Cooperation among established powers can reverse this result when credible arrangements allow them to manage the strategic consequences of suppression. Historical evidence from the American Revolution, China’s nuclear emergence, and U.S.–Soviet bargaining over West German nuclear capabilities illustrates the mechanisms and their limits. The analysis shows how rivalry among established powers can protect vulnerable rising states and thereby facilitate changes in the international distribution of power.

04be1a0d28:117498cdaa5d8ee8.title: Reassessing the 2000s Housing Cycle After Two Decades of Research -- by Adam Guren
04be1a0d28:117498cdaa5d8ee8.summary: What caused the 2000s housing cycle? This article synthesizes two decades of research, including reduced-form empirics and structural models. Although often contentious, the literature coheres once one accounts for each study’s timing, place, methodology, and measurement. The cycle was a perfect storm that occurred in distinct stages. Starting in the late 1990s, fundamentals improved, and credit supply increased across the income distribution due to automated underwriting and financial deregulation. In the early 2000s, a decline in interest rates was followed by a further expansion in securitized and subprime credit, the origin of which remains controversial. This sequence of shocks produced a persistent boom that triggered two shifts in beliefs: average expectations became overly optimistic, pushing prices higher, and expectations diverged, fueling speculation. In the bust, prices overshot primarily due to mortgage defaults, which removed buyers and contracted credit supply. How these forces interact and how expectations form require further research.

04be1a0d28:b757b426a444de0b.title: From Importer to Exporter: Oil Shocks and the U.S. Economy -- by Diego R. Känzig, James H. Stock, Luca Zanotti
04be1a0d28:b757b426a444de0b.summary: We study how the shale revolution and the U.S. transition from petroleum importer to net exporter have changed the macroeconomic effects of oil shocks. Using oil supply news shocks identified from OPEC announcements, a time-varying model of the U.S. macroeconomy shows that the contractionary effects weakened over time and eventually became expansionary. State-dependent local projections link this change to the U.S. petroleum trade balance. The improvement goes beyond mechanical net export effects: as the terms-of-trade response turns more favorable, consumption, equity valuations, and activity strengthen broadly across sectors and regions, pointing to general-equilibrium income and wealth effects. A counterfactual analysis of the 2022 oil price surge implies sharply different paths for U.S. activity, prices, and monetary policy under the propagation mechanisms prevailing before the shale boom vs. the early 2020s.

04be1a0d28:3b5a67007201ed58.title: Financing the AI Buildout -- by Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh
04be1a0d28:3b5a67007201ed58.summary: Artificial intelligence is driving a large expansion in data center capacity, power infrastructure, and specialized computing equipment. We estimate that a 1 GW AI campus costs about $41 billion. A 188 GW U.S. buildout completed by 2032 would require total investment of nearly$9 trillion and amount to annual investment of 3.2 percent of GDP over 2025–2032. As hyperscaler capital expenditures outgrow internal cash flow, financing is shifting toward leases, joint ventures, project debt, private credit, securitization, and special-purpose vehicles. These structures expand funding capacity but also raise asset-level leverage, obscure contingent obligations, and expose investors to tenant concentration, technological obsolescence, execution delays, and uncertain residual values.

04be1a0d28:6bd9ffd2d0627ae0.title: Gang Crackdowns -- by Carlos Schmidt-Padilla, Nikita Melnikov, María Micaela Sviatschi
04be1a0d28:6bd9ffd2d0627ae0.summary: What are the consequences of restoring state authority in territories governed by criminal organizations? Combining household surveys and administrative records with detailed maps of former gang-controlled areas, we study how El Salvador’s 2022 State of Exception, which ended two decades of gang territorial control, reshaped Salvadoran society. We find that the removal of gang control integrated previously segmented labor markets, improving mobility, employment outcomes, household income, and financial inclusion. Areas with greater pre-2022 gang exposure also experienced larger increases in business formation and property investment. However, the legacy of criminal governance persists through residence-based discrimination: employers remain less willing to hire otherwise identical applicants from former gang-controlled neighborhoods. Finally, although overall support for the crackdowns remains high, individuals who witnessed police abuse report substantially greater distrust of the police and the national government, suggesting that abuses of state authority may undermine the political sustainability of tough-on-crime policies.

04be1a0d28:d398785c9b0ea01f.title: The Investment Channel of Monetary Policy: Disentangling Firm Heterogeneity -- by Thomas Drechsel, Daniel Lewis, Davide Melcangi, Laura Pilossoph
04be1a0d28:d398785c9b0ea01f.summary: To study monetary policy transmission at the firm level, researchers typically consider heterogeneity along a small number of firm characteristics, such as size or leverage. We instead estimate the full distribution of firms’ investment responses to monetary policy, using a clustering regression framework. Our novel approach captures multidimensional and unobservable heterogeneity across firms and time. We find that investment by most firms in most time periods responds little to monetary policy. Only about 5% of firm-time observations are associated with a strong response. We then investigate the sources of heterogeneity ex post. We find that most of the variation in investment sensitivity arises within firms over time. Although several firm characteristics predict responsiveness to monetary policy, the majority of heterogeneity remains unexplained by firm observables. We demonstrate that our empirical estimates provide new targets for disciplining structural models of firm heterogeneity.

04be1a0d28:a80d341ce281553c.title: Optimal Line-Drawing for Legal Rules -- by Jacob Goldin, David Weisbach
04be1a0d28:a80d341ce281553c.summary: Line drawing is a pervasive feature of legal systems. Across many domains, the applicable legal treatment turns on whether an activity falls above or below some threshold. We characterize the economic forces that determine the optimal placement of such thresholds, both generally and in specific legal settings involving monetary and non-monetary sanctions, prohibitions, and mandates. We apply our results to two important line-drawing questions in private law: the optimal due-care threshold for negligence liability and the optimal threshold for whether a shortfall in contract performance constitutes breach. In both applications, the optimal line takes the form of a population-level marginal cost-benefit rule, with the relevant costs and benefits weighted over the actors whose behavior the line induces to change.

40c94f9b29:0c24df0751808b58.title: A Nobel for Microfoundations
40c94f9b29:0c24df0751808b58.summary: This year, the Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel, colloquially called the Nobel Prize in Economics , went to Robert E. Hall of Stanford University and Michael Woodford of Columbia University for their work in “microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilization.” Those five words do not adequately describe their contributions. Hall and Woodford are macroeconomists whose major works emerged when macro was in crisis. Old school Keynesian economics had dominated economic policy discussions since the 1940s. Generally speaking, Keynesians advocated fiscal policy tools (specifically taxes and spending) to stabilize the economy. For about 20 years, those tools seemed to work. But starting in the late 1960s and through the 70s, the macroeconomic relationships broke down. A seemingly impossible confluence of rising inflation and high unemployment characterized this period. Keynesian spending policies were becoming impotent. Critics of Keynesianism rose, and macroeconomics called out for new theories. It was during this period that macroeconomics began to explore more microfoundations. That is, rather than treating the economy as a series of aggregates and their relations to one another, economists started to explore how aggregate macroeconomic factors were the results of individual behavior, institutions, and expectations. Stabilization policy could not be simply levers pulled or pushed by the policymaker. Rather, stabilization policy had to include theories on how people will react to such changes, as well as their expectations about the future. Models such as rational expectations, adaptive expectations, and the permanent income hypothesis were developed during this period as a means to explain why these Keynesian stabilization policies failed. One of the models that came out of this period was Milton Friedman’s Permanent Income Hypothesis. The basic idea is that people base their consumption decisions not just on current income…

40c94f9b29:a780bf86d4a4f4b9.title: The Great Fertility Collapse (with Jesus Fernandez-Villaverde)
40c94f9b29:a780bf86d4a4f4b9.summary: For the first time in human history, we’re not having enough children to keep the world’s population from falling. And fertility is collapsing fastest not in rich nations but in places like Colombia, Thailand, and Guatemala, upending decades of economic wisdom. Economist Jesus Fernandez-Villaverde tells EconTalk’s Russ Roberts that falling fertility has accelerated sharply over the past decade and defies easy explanation. Declining religiosity, smartphones and social media, soaring housing costs, and changing gender norms are popular, but unconfirmed, theories. Fernandez-Villaverde offers his own speculative answer, that modern life makes a third child costly and childlessness easy, but admits the puzzle is unsolved. What’s clearer is why it matters: as retirees become the dominant voting bloc, spending on pensions and health care crowds out roads, schools, and defense. Shrinking economies make public debt harder to service, and fewer births mean fewer scientists, artists, and inventors. (1 COMMENTS)

40c94f9b29:a54c6f82e5753273.title: Debt and Profit
40c94f9b29:a54c6f82e5753273.summary: An ordinary person can earn a paycheque, pay her taxes, cover living costs and mortgage payments, and perhaps even add to her savings — and at the end of the day she will still owe most of her mortgage. This is a normal state of affairs, and nobody finds it puzzling. Yet when a company reports profits alongside large amounts of debt, the reaction is often to question whether it’s really making money. After all, if a company is “truly” profitable, why is it in debt? The short answer is that debt is not the opposite of profit. Loss is the opposite of profit. This imagined contradiction is easier to resolve once we recognize that profit is a flow and debt is a stock. According to the SEC’s guide to financial statements, the income statement records revenues, expenses, and profit over a period, while the balance sheet records assets and liabilities — such as debt — at a point in time. In fact, debt and profit are entirely unrelated concepts. Imagine a firm borrows money to purchase a machine. When the loan arrives, the firm’s cash and debt rise by the same amount. When the purchase is made, the firm simply exchanges one asset (cash) for another (the machine). Neither transaction creates a profit or a loss. Over time, the machine may be used in productive activities that raise revenue. By the same token, depreciation in the machine’s value can lower profit over its useful life, and interest — the cost of managing debt — adds to expenditures for as long as the debt is outstanding. The best way to think about debt is as a contract that moves purchasing power across people and time. Savers give up control over their resources today, while borrowers promise principal and interest later in exchange for controlling those resources now. Banks and bond markets pool and match funds from many people, letting a single firm undertake a factory, railway, or phone network without first accumulating the cash itself. As Frédéric Bastiat put it, credit institutions “can make it easier…

40c94f9b29:b79d2bc5c55e544a.title: Addiction, Faith, and the Limits of Willpower (with Meghan O’Gieblyn)
40c94f9b29:b79d2bc5c55e544a.summary: Why do we keep doing things we know we shouldn’t? And is that really a failure of will? Author Meghan O’Gieblyn spent years trying to answer that question, first in response to her struggle with alcoholism and her loss of faith, and then by means of Simone Weil, William James, and Iris Murdoch, who argue that the will is powerless over the things we want to change most. Listen as she speaks with EconTalk’s Russ Roberts about her new memoir, Will and Attention , which explores why paying attention does what effort alone can’t, why we can reason ourselves into doing destructive things, and why the choices that most shape our lives are the “choices in between the choices,” or the ones we barely notice making at all.
