4a32a2255e:6b44000d8f244708.title: Unpacking place transformation
4a32a2255e:6b44000d8f244708.author: OECD
4a32a2255e:6b44000d8f244708.summary: Many communities across the OECD are struggling to keep pace with economic change. Persistent disparities in employment rates, skills mismatches and economic inactivity reflect a fractured geography of opportunities, and long-lasting effects of economic shocks and structural change. The consequences are not just economic, but also deeply personal, with potential to fuel disillusionment and to reinforce cycles of disadvantage. Yet, successful examples of transformation highlight that decline is not inevitable. Experiences from success stories can inform how to both better address scars from the past as well as more proactively adapt to future transitions. This paper provides a fresh perspective on place transformation, in particular one that better reflects the role of “soft infrastructure” like local leadership and place identity, bridges local and external drivers of change, and better integrates economic and social outcomes.

4a32a2255e:6ed835f06f6a9429.title: Relaxing Immigration Restrictions in a Peripheral Region: Evidence from Finnish North Karelia
4a32a2255e:6ed835f06f6a9429.author: Jeremias Nieminen
4a32a2255e:6ed835f06f6a9429.summary: Several countries use immigration liberalization as a place-based policy tool, but evidence on its regional effects remains almost entirely descriptive. We examine the causal impact of removing labor market testing (LMT) regulations for labor immigrants in all occupations in the remote Finnish region of North Karelia. The reform allowed firms to hire non-EU foreign workers in all occupations without first advertising jobs to domestic applicants, resulting in a 14% rise in the stock of immigrant workers. Using synthetic control and difference-in-differences methods, we estimate causal effects of the reform at the regional, municipal, firm establishment, and individual levels. The reform caused immigrant inflows to increase primarily in cities and in specific types of occupations, i.e., low-paying occupations and ISCO groups 5, 7, 8, and 9. Across the firm size distribution, the increases concentrate around the median and the top. We find little evidence that the policy had meaningful effects on other regional or municipal outcomes: immigration liberalization boosted labor supply without generating transformative medium-term regional effects.

4a32a2255e:1077669d0ec7db22.title: Playing Europe's hand: competitiveness, place and the high stakes of territorial myopia
4a32a2255e:1077669d0ec7db22.author: Dijkstra, Lewis
4a32a2255e:1077669d0ec7db22.summary: The European Union (EU) confronts a widening productivity gap with the United States (US) and China. Informed by the Draghi Report (2024), the emerging response is a bold but narrow one, dominated by massive investment in the technologies and sectors where Europe most conspicuously lags. This article argues that pursuing parity in areas where Europe shows considerable weakness is the wrong race. The surer path runs through Europe's existing strengths —its pharmaceutical hubs, aerospace clusters, machine-tool districts and chemical bases, among others— used not as a pretext for standing still but as a springboard for reinvention. This implies mobilising the potential of every European territory by climbing the complexity ladder, absorbing new technologies into living industrial ecosystems, and diversifying into related activities that grow organically out of existing capabilities. A differentiated, place-sensitive strategy built on path dependence, brownfield digitalisation and the deliberate strengthening of European chokepoints in strategic sectors offers a more durable route to competitiveness than chasing after American or Chinese shadows. Europe is not short of talent or invention: the problem lies in institutional barriers to integration, the weakness of its knowledge-to-innovation pipeline, and its chronic inability to help promising start-ups graduate into globally significant firms. Fix those, and the case for territorial myopia collapses. For if Europe is bound to struggle at imitation, it might as well succeed at being itself and, on its own terms, lead.

4a32a2255e:72d83801ff86b493.title: The Skyscraper Revolution: Global Economic Development and Land Savings
4a32a2255e:72d83801ff86b493.author: Remi Jedwab
4a32a2255e:72d83801ff86b493.summary: Tall buildings make up over 20% of real estate by value in the world's largest cities. Nonetheless, many governments constrain tall building construction, hindering urbanization and growth. Quantification for all cities worldwide using a canonical land use model disciplined with reduced form elasticity estimates indicates that eliminating existing height constraints would generate a welfare gain of 3.7% in developing economies. Aggregate land values would decline by 3.9%, incentivizing landowners to support height restrictions. Estimated elasticities of city population and built area with respect to aggregate city building heights are 0.13 and -0.16, reinforcing the quantitative evidence that tall buildings facilitate urban growth and compactness. Interactions between static demand factors and the geography of bedrock isolate 1975-2015 tall building construction driven by technology-induced reductions in the cost of height. Using indirect inference, we estimate a (congestion) elasticity of consumer welfare to urban density of -0.11.

4a32a2255e:87b3c2b5686737f0.title: Structural Amplification in UK Production Networks between 2017 and 2022
4a32a2255e:87b3c2b5686737f0.author: Antonio Haro-Banon
4a32a2255e:87b3c2b5686737f0.summary: The UK economy experienced three major shocks between 2017 and 2022&colon Brexit, the pandemic, and the European energy crisis. This paper asks whether these events changed the structure of the UK's production network, using detailed data covering 12 UK regions and 105 industries. A key finding is that conventional measures can be misleading. On the face of it, the UK economy appeared to become more interconnected over this period, with standard input&dashoutput multipliers rising by around 5&dash6 per cent. However, once inflation and sector-specific price changes are stripped out, that increase disappears. The UK's average multiplier was essentially unchanged. The more important change was structural. Measures of how shocks propagate through supply chains show that the production network became more amplifying and more concentrated, with most of this shift occurring in 2021&dash22. The evidence points overwhelmingly to the energy sector, especially electricity and gas, as the source of this change. Brexit&dashrelated effects appear smaller, while pandemic effects are diffuse. The policy lesson is that resilience depends not only on average interconnectedness but also on where influence is concentrated. The energy&dashprice shock exposed the extent to which a small number of strategically important sectors can reshape the transmission of disturbances across the wider economy. Monitoring these structural vulnerabilities may be as important as tracking headline measures of economic activity.

4a32a2255e:0be5b930dc5f730d.title: How an Economy Shrinks in Space: Concavity-on-Jobs and Upward Consolidation under Demographic Decline
4a32a2255e:0be5b930dc5f730d.author: Miki Ogawa
4a32a2255e:0be5b930dc5f730d.summary: When a country's population declines, the aggregate economy appears to contract on the intensive margin: industrial diversity intact, every industry a little smaller. At the regional level, contraction is uneven and takes the extensive form: entire industries disappear, one after another. The relevant unit is the city: industries are nested by size - the hierarchy property of industrial location - each viable only above a minimum population. Necessity industries' thresholds bunch at the low end, so a city's industry count - and its jobs - is sharply concave in size (concavity on jobs). A modest loss pushes a small city below many thresholds at once; a large core sheds a few specialized industries, one at a time. Lost industries consolidate upward to the next city large enough to host them; for the worker it means a step down to a lower-paid local job. To recover that income, workers move up to the apex - the only city hosting the full industry range. Studying Japan - two decades ahead of the OECD, Tokyo at its apex - with worker-level panel data on the young workers who carry the migration, a wage regression in real, housing-inclusive wages identifies a Tokyo-bound migration incentive that varies by origin, following concavity on jobs.

4a32a2255e:b2332a907c275cd9.title: Dinámicas de convergencia regional en las principales economías europeas
4a32a2255e:b2332a907c275cd9.author: Diana Posada Restrepo
4a32a2255e:b2332a907c275cd9.summary: En este documento se analizan las dinámicas de convergencia del PIB per cápita entre 98 regiones de España, Alemania, Francia e Italia durante el período 1998-2025. Empleando la metodología de Phillips y Sul (2007, 2009) se identifican seis clubes de convergencia. Los resultados revelan una heterogeneidad estructural: los clubes más avanzados, integrados principalmente por regiones alemanas, presentan niveles de PIB per cápita persistentemente superiores a la media muestral. Los clubes intermedios y bajos, compuestos en su mayoría por regiones francesas, italianas y españolas, convergen hacia equilibrios de menor renta relativa. Para estimar los determinantes del crecimiento de cada región se emplea un modelo de panel dinámico heterogéneo con efectos comunes. Los resultados sugieren que las disparidades regionales europeas no solo responden a diferencias en dotaciones de factores, sino también a la distinta capacidad de las regiones para convertir dichas dotaciones en crecimiento económico. En particular, el papel del capital humano y el stock de capital físico destacan como elementos clave en la explicación de estas divergencias.

33e1d7779a:d49c0f37a64c1683.title: Ukraine's Starlink restrictions raise suspicions of Musk, Trump retaliation
33e1d7779a:d49c0f37a64c1683.author: Barak Ravid
33e1d7779a:d49c0f37a64c1683.summary: The rupture between President Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky over last week's diesel deal deepened Wednesday after an Elon Musk -owned satellite system used by Ukraine unexpectedly restricted service — undercutting Ukraine's fight against Russia. Why it matters: The Ukrainian military uses SpaceX's Starlink satellite communications system to control and operate its reconnaissance and intercept drones. When it doesn't operate at full capacity, Ukraine's ability to gather intelligence, use interceptor drones and conduct long-range strikes against Russia is impeded. Service was partially restored on Wednesday, but Ukrainian officials were still searching for answers about why the service was throttled and who was responsible. The limitations came days after a new crisis erupted between the U.S. and Ukraine over Trump's agreement to lift sanctions on Russian oil sales. Zelensky criticized the move, then Trump called for Ukraine to elect a new president. A senior U.S. official said the Trump administration had nothing to do with the alleged Starlink service constraints. But Ukrainian officials remain suspicious. Driving the news: Ukrainian officials said SpaceX imposed the restrictions Tuesday night. The system turned off, they said, when a drone exceeded 160 kph. In some cases, it disconnected when the speed went over 80 kph. The Starlink restrictions came several hours after the Ukrainian military did not receive an early warning about a Russian ballistic missile attack. Ukrainian officials said the U.S. has provided such alerts over the last several years as part of intelligence sharing between the countries. U.S. officials pointed to a technical malfunction in the system, but Ukrainian officials suspect that it was a warning shot from the Trump administration. "We had massive [Russian] attacks today and it's a pity that we also had difficulties ... about Starlink and about intelligence and a lot of different surprises," Zelensky said at the top of…

33e1d7779a:0c925ea05951d9b9.title: AI tools are aiding would-be spies
33e1d7779a:0c925ea05951d9b9.author: Sam Sabin
33e1d7779a:0c925ea05951d9b9.summary: AI tools are now exacerbating a largely hidden problem that frontier AI companies have been contending with for years: the risk that employees will exploit their access to spy on their employers. Why it matters: The same AI tools that companies are racing to release can also help people plan crimes and develop the technology to carry them out, creating another security headache for the companies building them. Driving the news: Federal prosecutors charged Abdulrahman Alfozan, a Saudi national who has been an OpenAI engineer since July 2025, with allegedly attempting to intercept private conversations at OpenAI. Around Sept. 30, the company found a "surreptitious audio recording device" that was plugged into a USB port in the back of a television in an executive conference room. OpenAI said in a post on X that it used its own AI models to help "understand the device and where it had come from." Zoom in: Investigators allege Alfozan used AI tools to research company meeting rooms and develop recording equipment, according to an FBI affidavit . Alfozan used a "productivity agent" to ask basic information about OpenAI's offices, the documents say. Those queries included: "What meeting was this presented at and when was it record?," "List meeting rooms in (company) that are 6+", and "can you list today's meeting in this room." Investigators also said that an AI chatbot account tied to his spouse asked the model to build a "continuous audio recorder" and to add "browser access an controls," as well as encrypt the memory card where the recordings were saved. The complaint didn't say whether any sensitive conversations were successfully recorded. The big picture: This is just the latest case where AI tools have helped people carry out alleged crimes. Prosecutors say they discovered a Nebraska man's use of ChatGPT before a bank robbery, including asking the model for assistance with stripping and repairing a handgun. He was sentenced to more than 10 years in prison in…

33e1d7779a:89ddc03eec32a715.title: DOJ gave California a voter list, a 48-hour deadline — and a threat of court action
33e1d7779a:89ddc03eec32a715.author: Avery Lotz
33e1d7779a:89ddc03eec32a715.summary: The Trump administration is threatening emergency court action unless California officials investigate potential ineligible voters within 48 hours and set aside ballots from anyone whose citizenship they cannot verify, according to two letters sent to state officials from the Justice Department. Why it matters: With voting already underway, President Trump 's DOJ could delay ballots from eligible Californians mistakenly flagged as noncitizens and set up a court fight just three weeks before Election Day. Driving the news: Acting Deputy Attorney General R. Trent McCotter sent a letter Tuesday to Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder/County Clerk Dean Logan along with a thumb drive of "likely noncitizens who were sent a vote-by-mail ballot," according to a copy of the letter shared with Axios. McCotter asks local officials to investigate their citizenship status by noon October 15. The letter did not say how many people are on the list. For anyone whose status can't be confirmed, DOJ asks the officials to "segregate—not cancel" those ballots and suspend signature verification or counting of any ballots already returned. DOJ also asks officials to withhold ballots from people on the list unless their citizenship has been confirmed. California Secretary of State Shirley Weber received a similar letter . Friction point: McCotter closed his letter with a threat: "If you cannot implement this process by then, given the ongoing federal election, the United States will have no choice but to seek emergency relief." What they're saying: "This should not be controversial, as the criminal statute is clear: only American citizens may vote in federal elections. It is a federal crime for noncitizens to vote in U.S. elections, and the DOJ is asking California to ensure that is not occurring," a DOJ spokesperson said in a statement. The California secretary of state's office and the Los Angeles County office did not respond to request for comment. The other side: "One must question…

33e1d7779a:365db38b7d7e88fd.title: ICE says no to automatic body-cams
33e1d7779a:365db38b7d7e88fd.author: Josephine Walker
33e1d7779a:365db38b7d7e88fd.summary: ICE is rejecting a Government Accountability Office recommendation for technology that automatically activates body cameras when weapons are drawn and safeguards to ensure agents record arrests, searches and detentions when required. Why it matters: The GAO warns that ICE risks losing crucial evidence on what happened during incidents involving force amid growing distrust over agent accountability in the wake of multiple fatal ICE shootings . The big picture: The GAO report found both CBP and ICE are struggling to manage their body-camera programs amid shifting deployment plans. CBP and ICE haven't updated their camera plans since 2022 and 2024, respectively. The plans fail to account for funding changes, expanded deployment needs and pauses in camera rollouts following one of Trump's executive orders that rescinded a Biden-era federal body-camera mandate. ICE's camera activation dispute is the central flashpoint in the GAO review, as DHS accepted all six other recommendations. CBP uses technology that automatically activates body cameras when officers draw firearms or turn on emergency lights, but ICE doesn't. Zoom in: At six of the 10 locations GAO reviewed, CBP and ICE personnel said they were unsure when they had to turn on their cameras. Some said camera use is "not mandated," "up to interpretation," and "has gray areas." Agents specifically reported uncertainty about whether they should record during "subpoena issuance, in-custody interviews, vehicle searches, undercover operations, and detainee transports." At five sites, people said they weren't sure how to use a newer camera model. The other side: DHS rejected the recommendation, arguing that automatic activation "presents significant operational risks, including inadvertent or false activations during routine movement." DHS warned that accidental activation could expose sensitive interactions with informants and victims or record people engaged in protected First Amendment activities. GAO pushed back,…

33e1d7779a:1bcb2bcb02fa8a07.title: Exclusive: White House probes claims of missing Kennedy Center money in "MAGA blood feud"
33e1d7779a:1bcb2bcb02fa8a07.author: Marc Caputo
33e1d7779a:1bcb2bcb02fa8a07.summary: President Trump has directed his White House counsel to examine explosive allegations dropped on him Friday in the Oval Office: Former Trump attorney Alina Habba told the president that another one of his top advisers — former Kennedy Center leader Ric Grenell — failed to deposit a multimillion-dollar donation that her billionaire husband made to the center a year ago, according to four senior administration officials and three insiders briefed on the controversy. 33e1d7779a:b7d2a188ed70fe5e.title: Americans are losing faith in their fellow voters
33e1d7779a:b7d2a188ed70fe5e.author: Herb Scribner
33e1d7779a:b7d2a188ed70fe5e.summary: Data: Gallup ; Chart: Axios Americans' trust in their fellow citizens' democratic judgment has fallen to its lowest recorded level in more than five decades, according to a new Gallup survey. The big picture: Americans' growing distrust of political leaders and institutions now extends to one another, with Democrats and Republicans showing similar levels of skepticism. By the numbers: 51% of U.S. adults have a great deal or fair amount of trust in Americans as a whole to make democratic judgments, per Gallup. That's the lowest reading since Gallup began tracking the measure in 1974. The distrust cuts across party lines: 53% of Democrats, 51% of Republicans and 49% of independents trust Americans' ability to make democratic decisions. Flashback: Trust stood at 86% in 1976 and 78% in both 2002 and 2005. Trust has stayed below 60% since 2018, according to Gallup. State of play: Americans have more trust in their local government (67%) and state government (55%) than in their fellow citizens' democratic judgment (51%). The survey also found that 42% of Americans trust politicians who hold or seek public office, while 33% trust the news media. Zoom out: Americans' confidence in major U.S. institutions, including Congress, the presidency and the banking system, has also fallen to historically low levels. Methodology: Gallup surveyed 1,000 U.S. adults by landline and cellphone Sept. 1–17, 2026; the weighting-adjusted margin of error was plus or minus 4 percentage points.

33e1d7779a:8d5c9fb239c0fd23.title: New inflation warning sign
33e1d7779a:8d5c9fb239c0fd23.author: Courtenay Brown
33e1d7779a:8d5c9fb239c0fd23.summary: America's inflation problem is becoming harder to contain, with new evidence Wednesday that price pressures are extending beyond the war-related energy shock rattling the global economy . Why it matters: Inflation is squeezing household budgets and dimming hopes for relief. It is also increasing the prospect that the Fed will have to raise interest rates further. What they're saying: "Higher energy costs are beginning to seep into broader services prices, increasing the risk that this inflation burst will persist," Fitch Ratings economist Olu Sonola wrote in a note. The Consumer Price Index report "stands out as the first of the year in which price pressure appeared to be showing up in most corners of the consumption basket at once," Glenmede's Jason Pride wrote. By the numbers: The CPI rose 0.6% in September from the prior month, accelerating from August's 0.4% increase. The index increased 3.7% in the 12 months through September, compared with 3.4% in the prior month. Gasoline prices surged 9% in September, accounting for more than half of the monthly jump in consumer prices. Core prices, which exclude food and energy, advanced 0.3% for the second consecutive month. The annual rate accelerated to 2.6% from 2.4%. The intrigue: Over the past three months, core CPI has risen at a 3.4% annualized rate, up notably from 2% in August — a sign that underlying inflation pressures are strengthening. Inflation was stubborn in parts of the services economy that are less directly exposed to the energy price surge. Shelter costs accelerated last month, rising 0.4%, while used car prices climbed 0.7%. Airfares jumped 1.2% as airlines grappled with soaring jet fuel costs. "Supercore" — a narrower measure of inflation that excludes housing and energy services — was hot again last month. Prices in that category have risen at a nearly 4.6% annualized rate over the past three months. The big picture: Top Fed officials in recent days have played down the urgency of another interest…

33e1d7779a:43cb81b6bda98bce.title: Social Security recipients will see rise in monthly payments next year
33e1d7779a:43cb81b6bda98bce.author: Neil Irwin
33e1d7779a:43cb81b6bda98bce.summary: Data: Social Security Administration; Chart: Neil Irwin/Axios Social Security recipients will see the largest rise in their monthly payments in four years in January, with a 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment. Driving the news: The Social Security Administration announced the 2027 COLA adjustment for 76 million recipients of retirement and disability benefits, which by law is calculated based on the Consumer Price Index for the July-through-September quarter. That will increase the average retiree's benefits by $900 a year, or $75 a month. The agency also said that the cutoff for Social Security taxes will rise to $192,300 in 2027, from $184,500 this year. Income above that threshold is not subject to payroll tax. How it works: The adjustment is, by statute, determined by the year-over-year change in CPI for the third quarter. Thus, the September data released this morning was the final input needed to calculate the adjustment. Between the lines: The adjustment will mean more nominal income for seniors and disability recipients, amounting to a mild fiscal stimulus come January. However, it also accelerates Social Security's looming fiscal problems, with its trust fund scheduled to expire in six years. The most recent projections issued by the program's trustees assumed a 0.9 percentage point lower COLA for 2027, the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget notes.

33e1d7779a:8126cc7715c56735.title: Inflation heats up as gas prices surge
33e1d7779a:8126cc7715c56735.author: Courtenay Brown
33e1d7779a:8126cc7715c56735.summary: Data: Bureau of Labor Statistics ; Chart: Courtenay Brown/Axios U.S. inflation picked up in September as soaring energy prices added to already stubborn price pressures, the Labor Department said on Wednesday. Why it matters: The latest Consumer Price Index shows that the inflation fight is far from over — and makes further Federal Reserve interest rate hikes more likely as Americans struggle with higher costs. By the numbers: CPI rose 0.6% in September from the prior month, with the annual inflation rate at 3.7%, the government said. That compares with a 0.4% monthly increase and a 3.4% annual rate in August. Core prices, which exclude volatile food and energy costs, gained 0.3% on the month, compared with a similar monthly gain in August. In the 12 months through September, core CPI rose 2.6%, up from 2.4% the prior month. Zoom in: The latest figures capture the toll of the Middle East war on American consumers as disruptions to global energy supplies push up fuel prices. Gasoline prices spiked 9.1% in September after climbing 3.9% in August, when they accounted for more than a third of the monthly increase in consumer prices. Prices for shelter, one of the largest components of the index, increased 0.4%, compared with a 0.3% gain in August. Food prices were flat, compared with a slight 0.1% increase the previous month. Zoom out: The surge in fuel prices has prompted extraordinary measures from the Trump administration, particularly as soaring diesel costs threaten to push up prices for goods transported across the country . President Trump temporarily eased restrictions on tax-exempt diesel and lifted some U.S. sanctions on Russian fuel to boost global diesel supplies. Airline fares surged 1.2% in September — bringing the annual increase to 22% — as higher jet fuel costs put pressure on ticket prices. What to watch: The Social Security Administration is set to announce the 2027 cost-of-living adjustment for millions of retirees, based on inflation figures…

33e1d7779a:17ab65c23eb350cd.title: Apple bets AI can finally make us want a smart home
33e1d7779a:17ab65c23eb350cd.author: Ina Fried
33e1d7779a:17ab65c23eb350cd.summary: Apple's big new hardware bet for the AI era is here, and it's a...smart display? Why it matters : Cue the time machine and let's head back to 2014, when Amazon's Alexa shocked the tech world and led us to imagine a Jetsons-style home would be ours in the near future. It wasn't, but Apple believes it could come soon. The iPhone maker is betting that modern AI can finally make good on that vision, unveiling a slew of new smart home devices Tuesday. Between the lines: While the smart home has largely failed to live up to its promise, modern AI could help address its biggest shortcoming: Getting devices to just work without requiring users to become amateur IT experts. Apple's new products emphasize easy setup and integration with its existing ecosystem, while AI could help diagnose problems and coordinate devices. "The capabilities that AI would bring in helping make sure that these devices can solve their own problems and work together is really interesting to me," Paul Gagnon, a vice president at market research firm Circana, told Axios. Driving the news: Apple's announcements Tuesday included a new smart display, a revamped speaker, an updated streaming device and a collection of connected home accessories developed with partners. HomeView: Apple's new $299 smart display features a 7-inch screen and an AI-powered Siri that can respond to requests, control connected devices and recognize different household members to deliver personalized information. It will ship next month and comes in two versions, one that can hang on a wall and the other, a tabletop device reminiscent of the iMac G4. Apple Home Collection: Apple worked with LG and Schneider Electric on smart locks, doorbells, cameras and thermostats designed to work together through Apple's Home app and Siri. The big picture: The AI hardware race is taking two different paths: Making familiar devices substantially smarter and creating entirely new kinds of gadgets. Amazon and Google have been incorporating…

33e1d7779a:674f9298fcd3cabe.title: AI's extreme heat challenge is moving from prediction to protection
33e1d7779a:674f9298fcd3cabe.author: Rebecca Falconer
33e1d7779a:674f9298fcd3cabe.summary: Cities and researchers are using AI to map and predict extreme heat risk, but new research suggests it's used far more to identify where people are in danger than to help officials respond. Why it matters: As climate change intensifies extreme heat, better predictions won't protect vulnerable communities unless governments can turn them into action. U.S. deaths associated with high temperatures rose 53% from an annual average of 2,670 in 2000–2009 to more than 4,000 in 2010–2020, according to a 2025 Yale study . Driving the news: A study published in Climate Risk Management examined existing research on how AI and machine learning are being used to manage extreme heat. Of the research papers reviewed, 98.4% focused on prediction and 59.2% on prevention. That's compared with just 10.4% on response, 3.2% on recovery and 1.6% on preparedness — a disparity the authors call a "research-to-implementation gap." The research is heavily focused on using AI to forecast dangerous heat and identify who's at risk, with far less attention on how it can help officials decide what to do next. "Where AI can actually add value is where prediction is central to the decision-making, and that's in scale or providing more granularity," said Karishma V. Patel, a RAND policy researcher who co-authored the study. State of play: Turning sophisticated heat predictions into government action requires more than advanced models. Cornell researcher Jennah Gosciak told Axios that having "robust data systems" that can ingest data from a variety of sources and then make it usable to practitioners "is most of the battle here." Case in point: Google in June announced it had expanded its AI-powered Heat Resilience data from an initial 14-city pilot to more than 50 cities worldwide, giving urban planners building-level data to help target heat interventions. The data uses AI and high-resolution imagery to map roof reflectivity down to individual buildings. Google said data from the pilots helped…

33e1d7779a:7202223420e7905c.title: Trump plays Russian roulette on eve of midterms
33e1d7779a:7202223420e7905c.author: Zachary Basu
33e1d7779a:7202223420e7905c.summary: President Trump is indulging his fondness for Vladimir Putin at a moment of acute political peril, forcing Republicans in the midterms to take cover as he showers Moscow with one-sided concessions. Why it matters: With just three weeks until the election, Trump is rekindling a decade-long, scandal-scarred relationship with a dictator reviled by most Americans — including his own supporters. Driving the news: Since speaking with Putin on Friday, Trump has embarked on a remarkable five-day campaign of diplomatic concessions and cover for Russia — sparking bipartisan blowback just as voters prepare to cast their ballots. On Friday, Trump announced a deal to unleash millions of tons of Russian diesel onto global markets, easing sanctions designed to starve Moscow's war revenues. On Saturday, Trump lashed out at Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky for striking Russian refineries and demanded that Kyiv replace its leader. On Sunday, Trump blindsided Zelensky by declaring an immediate "energy ceasefire." Russia has continued attacking Ukrainian energy infrastructure, with no apparent consequences from Washington. On Monday, Trump dismissed months of intelligence-based reports that Russia was enabling Iran's war effort by supplying information about U.S. military assets. On Tuesday, Trump doubled down on the diesel deal and brushed off concerns that the proceeds could finance Russia's war machine, even as GOP senators labeled it a "betrayal" and "a gift to our adversary." Between the lines: The benefits to Russia are clear. Far less apparent is what Trump's concessions accomplish for American security, European allies or his own political fortunes. For America: Energy analysts doubt the diesel deal will meaningfully ease fuel prices sent soaring by the Iran war. For Europe: Washington is breaking ranks with a NATO alliance confronting a historic threat environment , as Russia escalates its hybrid campaign of sabotage, cyberattacks and drone incursions. For Republicans:…

33e1d7779a:87a7bf92b1db9148.title: Exclusive: AI safety money floods into political races
33e1d7779a:87a7bf92b1db9148.author: Maria Curi
33e1d7779a:87a7bf92b1db9148.summary: Advocates for AI safety and regulation are emerging as a force in U.S. elections, spending nearly $50 million this election cycle on candidates who favor regulation, a new analysis shared exclusively with Axios shows. Why it matters: The safety spending points to the unusual power dynamics in the AI race, where researchers shape policy and regulation in ways that differ at times from the priorities of the companies where they work. The researchers add to the advocacy and giving of an array of AI safety groups that have been well-funded for years, including from Coefficient Giving, a philanthropy with close ties to many top AI executives, especially at Anthropic. Driving the news: AI safety groups and individual donors have spent $48 million this cycle on Democratic and Republican races, according to new figures shared first with Axios. That includes donations from researchers, such as OpenAI's Juan Felipe Cerón Uribe and Redwood's Aryan Bhatt. It also includes Guardrails Alliance, a tech-worker backed AI safety group, which has raised $11.7 million between its super PAC and 501(c)(4). The big picture: Taking AI industry money has grown complicated due to viral warnings of catastrophic AI risk from the very same industry developing it and data center NIMBYism mobilizing communities in blue and red districts alike. OpenAI President Greg Brockman pulled a planned second $25 million donation from Leading the Future, a super PAC backed by tech execs and investors, in part because of an internal revolt at OpenAI. Forces favoring AI acceleration — who earlier in the year appeared to favor veiled threats to pro-regulation candidates — haven't spent as much as opponents expected, and safety advocates see an opportunity to fill the void. Zoom in: Jacob Eliosoff, who runs the cryptocurrency investment fund Calibrated Markets, said he decided to engage in political giving related to AI after he saw early fundraising and candidate advocacy from Leading the Future. Eliosoff, an…

33e1d7779a:42a741cd61db5d06.title: Ossoff rejects 2028 buzz amid bruising night of Senate debates
33e1d7779a:42a741cd61db5d06.author: Stef W. Kight
33e1d7779a:42a741cd61db5d06.summary: Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.) delivered another debate performance tailor-made for social media Tuesday night, feeding the presidential speculation he insists is entirely misplaced. Why it matters: A darling of the Democratic internet and a favorite to win the party's nomination in 2028, Ossoff emphatically ruled out a White House bid and pledged to serve a full six-year Senate term if re-elected. In Georgia, Ossoff and Collins traded vicious personal attacks throughout their second and final debate, reprising a feud that has become a viral spectacle online. Ossoff demanded , referring to Collins' son-in-law, an alleged white nationalist influencer. Susan Collins cast her independence from Trump as a political asset, arguing that her willingness to challenge the president — and work with him when necessary — has delivered for her state. Collins cited her nine votes to end the Iran war, opposition to Trump's Big Beautiful Bill and roughly $1.5 billion in federal funding secured for Maine projects. Democratic…

33e1d7779a:f95f468118db8b1b.title: Judge orders White House to reinstate press access until litigation concludes
33e1d7779a:f95f468118db8b1b.author: Sara Fischer
33e1d7779a:f95f468118db8b1b.summary: A federal judge on Tuesday ruled the Trump administration must continue to grant CNN, MS NOW and Politico access to the White House grounds while the lawsuit filed by the three news organizations continues. Why it matters: It marks a major win for the news outlets as it maintains their White House access and signals the judge believes their legal claims could succeed on their merits. Judge Timothy Kelly, an appointee of President Trump, awarded a temporary restraining order to the plaintiffs on Sept. 24 that mandated the White House reinstate the outlets' credentials for 14 days. Last week, Kelly extended that through Oct. 13. The preliminary injunction preserves the outlets' access until the case is resolved, which could take weeks, months or years. Zoom in: "Defendants (except for President Trump) and their agents, representatives, and all persons or entities acting in concert with them, shall not execute, implement, or enforce the September 18, 2026, decision to revoke the White House 'hard pass' press credentials held by employees of CNN, MS NOW, and POLITICO," the court order from Judge Kelly said. Yes, but: The judge's ruling doesn't guarantee that the plaintiffs have access to key areas, such as the Oval Office and Air Force One. The White House has continued to bar CNN and Politico journalists from press pool assignments onboard Air Force One, despite the temporary restraining order reinstating their credentials. A different White House lawsuit, brought by the Associated Press, could help clarify the extent of the president's power to bar reporters from those types of spaces. That case is ongoing . Catch up quick: The news outlets sued the White House, arguing it violated their First Amendment rights by blocking them in retaliation for their reporting and discriminating against their viewpoints. They also argued their Fifth Amendment rights were violated as they were banned without due process. The temporary restraining order and the preliminary injunction…

33e1d7779a:ce0f8ccc08697f8c.title: Mike Johnson's Latino voter problem keeps getting worse
33e1d7779a:ce0f8ccc08697f8c.author: Hans Nichols
33e1d7779a:ce0f8ccc08697f8c.summary: House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) needs Latino voters to stick with Republicans as they did in 2024. But new polling shows they're drifting back toward Democrats at levels not seen in years. Why it matters: Latino voters souring on President Trump has been part of the mood music of the president's second term. Democrats hope this helps them replicate the landslide from Trump's first midterm in 2018. The big picture: Democrats have their widest lead of the year against Republicans, 57% to 31%, on the generic congressional ballot, according to new polling from Equis Research. In battleground districts, Democrats lead 62%–38% among likely Latino voters in two-way races, ahead of the party's 2022 level of 57%. That's well above the 49% of Latinos who voted Democratic in 2024, but below the 67% who backed Democrats in 2018, according to Equis , a leading authority on Latino voting behavior. Zoom in: Republicans were convinced that Trump's undeniable gains in 2024 represented the beginnings of a real realignment, but poll after poll this year has indicated that Latino voters haven't found a permanent home in the GOP. In Florida, GOP Rep. María Elvira Salazar has addressed Trump directly in a campaign ad about his immigration crackdown. The Equis survey, conducted Sept. 23–Oct. 2, provides fresh evidence of Trump's declining support among Latino voters. Trump's approval rating stands at just 30%, compared with 65% disapproval. That's a 35-point deficit — and a new low in Equis surveys. Between the lines: Economic concerns — and rising gas prices — are driving much of the dissatisfaction, particularly the cost of living. 76% of Latino voters disapprove of Trump's handling of the cost of living, which 52% identify as their top issue. 54% trust Democrats more on the economy, compared with 33% who trust Republicans. That gives Democrats a 21-point advantage on the economy, up from just 7 points in February. The bottom line: Latino voters helped put Trump back in the White…

33e1d7779a:a009dec71825a536.title: Democrats fear "more October surprises" after "bullshit" raid on Ilhan Omar's home
33e1d7779a:a009dec71825a536.author: Andrew Solender
33e1d7779a:a009dec71825a536.summary: Congressional Democrats' private text chains lit up with fear and anger on Monday after Department of Homeland Security agents searched Rep. Ilhan Omar's (D-Minn.) home in Washington, D.C. Why it matters: The search came less than a month before the midterms , immediately setting off alarm bells among Democrats that "more October surprises" could be coming, as one senior Democrat told Axios. Rep. Becca Balint (D-Vt.) told Axios: "We expect more of this kind of thing." Driving the news: Homeland Security Investigations "executed a judicially authorized search warrant" on Omar's home as part of an ongoing immigration probe, the Justice Department said in a statement. DOJ has not detailed the scope or subject of the search warrant. Fox News reported the investigation concerns Omar's immigration paperwork. She came to the United States in 1995 as a 12-year-old refugee from Somalia. Omar's office and Democratic House leadership quickly denounced the action as an "abuse of power," with a spokesperson for Omar saying she "has done nothing wrong." What we're hearing: "People are outraged. ... [This is] what authoritarian tyrants and dictators do," said the senior House Democrat, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to relay colleagues' private conversations. Another House Democrat told Axios "the chatter on texts" is that "folks are irate." Zoom out: Democrats allege the raid fits into a broader pattern of Trump using federal resources to boost Republicans and target his political opponents. DHS became embroiled in controversy just last week after a statement targeting Pennsylvania Democrat Janelle Stelson, which critics said violates federal laws restricting partisan activities by federal officials. Trump has also come under fire for using taxpayer funds to run campaign-style television ads touting him and his administration in the run-up to the midterms. What they're saying: "President Trump will keep trying to intimidate and bully Americans ahead of the midterms,"…

33e1d7779a:dac0d974cdd3b5a6.title: Bank of America hit with $1.2 billion penalty over money laundering allegations
33e1d7779a:dac0d974cdd3b5a6.author: Courtenay Brown
33e1d7779a:dac0d974cdd3b5a6.summary: The Treasury Department on Tuesday announced more than $1.2 billion in penalties against Bank of America for years of failures to report suspicious transactions and address shortcomings in its anti-money-laundering program. Why it matters: The action includes the third-largest penalty in Treasury history. What they're saying: "Today's actions send a clear message that even the biggest financial institutions are not above the law," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a press release . The big picture: The civil action comes less than a week after federal regulators fined American Express $350 million over similar failures to detect and report suspected money laundering. Zoom in: Bank of America admitted to willfully violating federal anti-money-laundering laws — including requirements to maintain adequate safeguards and report suspicious transactions. Regulators said the bank failed to properly monitor trillions of dollars in transactions, resulting in more than $5 billion in suspicious activity that was either unreported or reported late. More than $1 billion involved potential national security and other high-priority risks — including Chinese money-laundering networks and suspected trade-based money laundering linked to the U.S.-Mexico border, regulators said. Of note: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency also assessed a $750 million civil penalty, the largest in the agency's history. Treasury also announced an $11.6 million settlement with Bank of America over hundreds of apparent violations of U.S. sanctions, including those targeting Russia and Iran. Flashback: Bank of America has been working to address deficiencies in its anti-money-laundering program since a December 2024 regulatory order. But regulators said significant problems persisted. Officials said the bank prioritized revenue while limiting compliance resources — at times relying on law enforcement and other outside sources to identify suspicious activity. The other side: In a…

33e1d7779a:70c1d9fad782a536.title: Rep. Ilhan Omar under investigation by Jeanine Pirro's office
33e1d7779a:70c1d9fad782a536.author: Avery Lotz
33e1d7779a:70c1d9fad782a536.summary: U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro said her office is probing Rep. Ilhan Omar's (D-Minn.) financial disclosures, the day after federal agents searched the congresswoman's Washington, D.C. home. The big picture: It's another example of the administration's escalating fight with the progressive lawmaker, who has clashed with the White House over its immigration crackdown — and whom President Trump has labeled as "crooked." Driving the news: Asked about a prior ethics probe into financial filings from the Office of Congressional Conduct, which her office said cleared Omar, Pirro said Tuesday on Fox News' "America Reports" that "is subject of an investigation as well." "It doesn't matter what the House does. It doesn't matter, you know, what this agency or that does. We're looking at the facts. Based upon the facts, we'll follow them wherever they take us," she said, and confirmed her office is handling the probe. Catch up quick: Federal agents searched Omar's home before dawn Monday as part of a separate immigration probe, Axios' Ben Berkowitz reported. Omar described the search in an X post as "an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement." Trump has repeatedly lashed out against Somali immigrants, including Omar — who he described in a post last year as "always wrapped in her swaddling hijab" and "the worst 'Congressman/woman'" in our Country." Zoom out: Omar's office pointed Axios to The Wall Street Journal's reporting last month that the Office of Congressional Conduct recommended that the House Ethics Committee dismiss allegations that she possibly violated House rules or law by reporting false or incomplete information in her financial disclosures. A disclosure filed last year listed Omar and her husband's assets as ranging from $6 million to $30 million. She later amended the form to reflect a much lower range, the Journal first reported, citing what her team said were accounting errors. Pirro's office did not respond to Axios's…

33e1d7779a:5afb7842aa817ee2.title: Pope Leo diagnosed with lung cancer
33e1d7779a:5afb7842aa817ee2.author: Josephine Walker
33e1d7779a:5afb7842aa817ee2.summary: Pope Leo has been diagnosed with lung cancer, the Vatican said Tuesday. Why it matters: The Vatican disclosed the pontiff's health news just hours after he underwent surgery to remove the lower lobe of his right lung . What they're saying: "The surgery was completed successfully, within the expected timeframe and as planned, and the holy father has returned to his room," per a Holy See Press Office statement published Tuesday. The office said in that statement it would provide more information shortly, and later followed up with news of Leo's diagnosis of lung adenocarcinoma, which they said tests "conducted beforehand" had led them to suspect. Driving the news: The first American pontiff was admitted to Rome's Agostino Gemelli University Hospital on Tuesday afternoon for surgery. "The Pope was in the operating room approximately three hours, while the operation itself lasted about 90 minutes. The doctors said it was successful and there were no complications," the statement said. The Catholic Church leader carried out his usual duties Monday and was greeted by supporters and patients at the hospital, according to the Vatican statement. Zoom in: Adenocarcinoma is the most common subtype of lung cancer, per the Cancer Center. It forms when the cells lining the outside of the lungs become cancerous. Its symptoms include persistent cough, shortness of breath and chest pain, amongst other things. Patients with adenocarcinoma don't always experience symptoms early on, and it is often detected during a scan for a medical reason unrelated to lung cancer. The big picture: Doctors discovered the nodule during routine medical checkups. Leo said Sunday that the nodule "was detected at a very early stage and is well localized." He thanked his supporters for their "spiritual closeness" and said he was entrusting himself to their prayers. Go deeper: Pope Leo to have "nodule" removed from lung Editor's note: This story has been updated with information about Leo's diagnosis.

33e1d7779a:118abdefe6df45c1.title: Inside Trump, Netanyahu's dilemma: Strike Iran before elections or wait
33e1d7779a:118abdefe6df45c1.author: Marc Caputo
33e1d7779a:118abdefe6df45c1.summary: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and President Trump last week discussed the possibility of launching a major new operation against Iran before the Israeli and U.S. elections, according to two U.S. officials, one Israeli official and a fourth source with knowledge of the matter. Netanyahu said during the call that he was concerned about Israeli intelligence indicating Iran was taking troubling steps to reconstitute its nuclear program, according to the Israeli official. The Israeli leader's call with Trump about the possible attack took place before Trump said he would not strike Iran ahead of the midterms. Why it matters: Resuming major combat operations in Iran would inject a volatile new issue into the Oct. 27 Israeli elections and the U.S. midterms a week later. But the Israeli and U.S. militaries are still on alert and concluding preparations to be ready in case he changes his mind, sources said. " Bibi seems to want to go in again. He has talked to the president about it a couple times, and the president has said, 'Well, you know, Bibi, go ahead and get ready.' But there's really no commitment. 'Go ahead and get ready' is maybe now, maybe later, maybe never," a U.S. official said. A White House official said it's "false" that Trump and Netanyahu discussed resuming the war. "The President has said that we will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the midterm elections," the person said. Netanyahu's office said that "the prime minister maintains regular contact with President Trump and senior U.S. administration officials and does not comment on the content of their conversations." Driving the news: Netanyahu has had several calls with Trump over the last two weeks about returning to major combat operations in Iran. According to the sources, Netanyahu and Trump spoke about a potential joint U.S.-Israeli operation that would hit military and nuclear targets. Netanyahu expressed concern about steps Israel believes Iran is taking to reconstitute…

33e1d7779a:d1656610c9283ba7.title: Hegseth wants a livestream execution. Here's how firing squads work
33e1d7779a:d1656610c9283ba7.author: Herb Scribner
33e1d7779a:d1656610c9283ba7.summary: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth plans to livestream the December execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan by using a firing squad, one of the rarest forms of capital punishment in the United States. Why it matters: The planned livestream would mark the first public U.S. execution in roughly 90 years, but it has already drawn scrutiny , with President Trump expressing doubt it'll happen. Catch up quick: Hegseth said Oct. 8 that Hasan, who was convicted of killing 13 people in the 2009 shooting , will be executed in December, and the execution will be livestreamed. Trump has expressed apparent uneasiness despite giving his initial endorsement , Axios' Marc Caputo reported. House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) expressed some concerns, too, while Vice President Vance said he wouldn't watch if it were aired. Zoom out: Execution by firing squad is rare, with only six since capital punishment resumed in 1977, per the Death Penalty Information Center. . The U.S. military last executed someone by firing squad in 1945, when it executed Pvt. Eddie Slovik for desertion in France, per NPR . The military's last execution was in 1961, when it hanged John A. Bennett . How a firing squad works State of play: The Pentagon hasn't disclosed its firing squad procedures for Hasan's execution and didn't respond to Axios' request for comment Tuesday. Past executions offer a glimpse of what the method typically involves. How it works: The procedure typically begins with a prisoner strapped to a chair placed before a wall and surrounded by sandbags to absorb blood. A medical professional will typically mark a target over the prisoner's heart, while a black hood covers the prisoner's head. The shooters fire simultaneously, aiming at the heart, from a set distance away from the prisoner. If shooters miss the heart, the prisoner can still die from blood loss. Zoom in: States have different approaches to the firing squad method. For example, Utah uses five shooters, one of whom has a blank…

33e1d7779a:9f9119fc1b2b3149.title: Russian diesel deal "a betrayal," bipartisan coalition says
33e1d7779a:9f9119fc1b2b3149.author: Avery Lotz
33e1d7779a:9f9119fc1b2b3149.summary: President Trump's deal to lift sanctions on Russia to increase diesel supplies "is a betrayal of the people of Ukraine" and "a gift to our adversary," a bipartisan coalition of senators wrote in a letter admonishing the agreement. Why it matters: The decision to turn to Vladimir Putin in an attempt to ease the diesel crunch is piling onto Republican headaches ahead of the midterms and fueling fresh friction between the U.S. and Ukraine. What they're saying: The deal "will not achieve just ends, nor will it benefit Americans," the senators warned, urging Trump to withdraw from it and ramp up the economic pressure on Russia as called for in a sanctions bill named for the late Sen. Lindsey Graham that he signed into law last month. While record-shattering diesel and gas prices are squeezing key industries and American households, the lawmakers argued that "allowing Russian-origin diesel into global markets will offer limited to no relief to Americans." Analysts have expressed doubt that the levels Trump pitched will meaningfully sway prices, Axios' Ben Geman reports . However, the lawmakers argued that it will "undoubtedly finance" Russia's war "and advance its security cooperation with China, Iran, and North Korea." The fine print: The signers are Sens. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.), Thom Tillis (R-NC), Jeanne Shaheen (D-NH), Susan Collins (R-Maine), Dick Durbin (D-Ill.), Alan Armstrong (R-Okla.), Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI), Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska), Jack Reed (D-RI), Chris Coons (D-Del.), Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.) and John Cornyn (R-Texas). The White House did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment. Zoom out: That bipartisan coalition has fellow dissenters on the Hill, including members of the president's party who swiftly condemned the deal. Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick (R-Pa.) vowed over the weekend to force a vote to block Russian oil purchases, predicting that "it will pass overwhelmingly." Retiring Rep. Don Bacon (R-Neb.) told Axios' Andrew Solender he…

33e1d7779a:2880876fc5711fe9.title: Companies are building with AI — and exposing new security risks
33e1d7779a:2880876fc5711fe9.author: Sam Sabin
33e1d7779a:2880876fc5711fe9.summary: The amount of AI-related infrastructure exposed to the public internet jumped 63% in nine months, according to new Censys data shared first with Axios. Why it matters: The AI boom isn't just creating new models and chatbots. It's creating a sprawling layer of software that companies will also need to inventory, patch and secure. Threat level: Many of these tools connect AI applications to sensitive corporate data and other services, creating potential entry points for hackers looking to access company systems. "It's a little bit beyond just like the tool itself, but these [tools] talk to some really sensitive systems," Emily Austin, a principal researcher at Censys and co-author of the report, told Axios. The big picture: Censys identified nearly 268,000 internet-facing systems running 44 different AI-related products as of July, up from roughly 164,000 in October 2025. These include the software used to connect AI models to databases, corporate applications and other services. Between the lines: The ease of building and hosting AI applications is making it harder for companies to keep track of what software employees are using and whether it's secure. Censys CEO Zakir Durumeric told Axios that companies were already struggling to keep track of their existing software even before employees started building their own AI applications. These new AI apps can often connect to sensitive company information, such as emails, financial records and internal databases. Zoom in: The most widely exposed product was n8n, a workflow automation platform that can connect AI agents to other applications and services. Censys found nearly 114,000 internet-facing deployments of n8n, including roughly 77,000 running software versions affected by at least one recently disclosed critical vulnerability. Researchers also found more than 54,000 exposed control panels for OpenClaw, an open-source AI agent that users can connect to personal accounts and other services. Yes, but: The findings…

33e1d7779a:9bcba8da70941702.title: Europe's alternative to Trump's China trade war
33e1d7779a:9bcba8da70941702.author: Courtenay Brown
33e1d7779a:9bcba8da70941702.summary: Europe is testing a new response to China Shock 2.0 , betting that it can confront Beijing's export juggernaut without resorting to President Trump's tariff-heavy approach. Why it matters: More of the world is beginning to confront the threat that China's industrial overcapacity poses to their industries. But protecting individual sectors will not solve the bigger problem: China's factories are cranking out far more than its own economy can absorb. Driving the news: The European Union and China struck a preliminary deal on Friday to sharply limit Chinese hybrid vehicle exports to Europe. The EU plans to initially cap Chinese hybrid and plug-in hybrid imports at 350,000 annually, potentially starting as early as December. The cap would more than halve projected Chinese hybrid shipments, which were on track to reach roughly 800,000 this year, an EU official told reporters . Imports totaled 302,000 in 2025. (Chinese officials Monday noted that the deal still allows its automakers to increase shipments from last year's levels.) Vehicles exceeding the quota would be blocked rather than face additional tariffs. The backdrop: France and Germany last week proposed giving Brussels sweeping new powers to restrict market access over unfair trade practices, a striking shift for Germany, which opposed EU tariffs on Chinese EVs in 2024. European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen warned in her annual address last month that the bloc's trade deficit with China had reached a "tipping point." "Some say the second China shock is looming. But it's already here," von der Leyen said. What they're saying: EU leaders are considering tougher powers to confront Chinese trade practices, including one resembling the authority Washington has used to impose sweeping tariffs on Chinese goods. The agreement could dampen momentum for harsher measures, making member states "hesitant this week to rock the boat," Daniel Mullaney, an Atlantic Council senior fellow and former U.S. trade…

33e1d7779a:66922b3388248d93.title: White House pushes out Kimberly Guilfoyle after misconduct reports
33e1d7779a:66922b3388248d93.author: Josephine Walker
33e1d7779a:66922b3388248d93.summary: The White House has asked Kimberly Guilfoyle , the U.S. ambassador to Greece, to resign after reports of alleged misconduct before and during her diplomatic posting. Why it matters: The potential removal of the president's longtime political ally and former fiancée of his son Donald Trump Jr. follows a series of Wall Street Journal reports alleging she used her political connections to seek financial favors and promote private business interests. Guilfoyle has denied any wrongdoing. White House press secretary Katie Zacharia confirmed the request on Tuesday during her first press briefing. "She has been a wonderful asset to the team and we wish her well," Zacharia said. Guilfoyle's removal isn't entirely surprising, as Trump told reporters yesterday that he was "looking at" firing Guilfoyle following the allegations: "We're not happy," he said. Those comments follow a senior U.S. official telling AP that Trump and Rubio were "extremely pissed off" about the reports and were considering dismissing her. The U.S. Embassy in Athens and the State Department did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment. Zacharia declined to answer additional questions about Guilfoyle and referred reporters to the president. It wasn't immediately clear if Guilfoyle has resigned. Catch up quick: The WSJ's Oct. 8 report said that Guilfoyle allegedly sought $100,000 from a Trump donor to pay a credit card bill before her Senate confirmation hearing, and offered access to Trump administration officials in return. The donor did not make the payment. An earlier investigation alleged she promoted the interests of a Greek construction and energy company and allowed its lobbyist into private diplomatic meetings. The WSJ also reported that recordings captured Guilfoyle allegedly discussing private jet travel and luxury hospitality provided by wealthy Greek businessmen. For the record: Guilfoyle's lawyer disputed the authenticity of messages the WSJ cited and the U.S. Embassy in Athens…

33e1d7779a:524228311da79e07.title: Five things to watch after Trump's Russian diesel deal
33e1d7779a:524228311da79e07.author: Ben Geman
33e1d7779a:524228311da79e07.summary: President Trump is turning to Vladimir Putin to help ease a global diesel crunch, setting up a clash between Washington's energy priorities and its efforts to pressure Russia over its invasion of Ukraine. Why it matters: The fuel shortage is among the most severe effects of the Iran war and Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries. Average U.S. diesel prices remain far above $6 per gallon, adding to GOP headwinds in the midterm elections. Trump says his deal will help bring costs down. Catch up quick: Trump on Friday claimed an agreement to bring escalating Russian exports, and the Treasury Department waived sanctions to help enable it. A few things to watch... The campaign trail. So far a few Republicans in close races — including Michigan Senate candidate Mike Rogers and Alaska Sen. Dan Sullivan — have criticized the agreement. Republicans already saddled with Trump's unpopular policies in the midterms now face another awkward choice: whether to back his diesel deal with a dictator many of them despise, Axios' Andrew Pantazi writes. The market. Diesel futures dipped after the announcement. But analysts expressed doubt that the levels Trump is claiming will meaningfully sway prices in the U.S. and elsewhere — if Russia indeed delivers. Per Trump's claim, Russia will "immediately" provide what amounts to 2.24 million barrels, followed 3.73 million next month (equivalent to around 124,000 barrels per day spread over a month), and then roughly double it thereafter. "In the near-term, it's hard to see the waiver helping global fundamentals for diesel much," writes economics and geopolitics analyst Rachel Ziemba. The global market currently has a deficit of about 1 million barrels per day, per market intel firm Kpler, and "Russia's ability to deliver additional barrels remains uncertain," writes Kpler's Michelle Brouhard. Capitol Hill. Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick (R-Pa.), one of those lawmakers in a close reelection fight, will try and force a House vote to block Russian…

33e1d7779a:f1f209fe14353bb4.title: Axios-Ipsos poll: "Medicare for All" support surges
33e1d7779a:f1f209fe14353bb4.author: Margaret Talev
33e1d7779a:f1f209fe14353bb4.summary: Supporters of "Medicare for All" now outnumber opponents by nearly 2-to-1, according to a new survey of U.S. adults from the Axios-Ipsos American Health Index . The big picture: Two-thirds of all survey respondents — and half of Republicans — said the federal government should be willing to spend more tax dollars to lower health care costs for Americans. Why it matters: With three weeks to go before the midterm elections, and private health insurance premiums and prescription prices crushing voters, these findings suggest a path for swing-state candidates who embrace socialized medicine. But the public's openness is driven more by desperation than by confidence in government. Affordability is foremost on most Americans' minds, and health care brings almost daily reminders of economic pressure. Between the lines: Survey respondents say they want more government intervention — but they trust those leaders less than ever. Trust in President Trump for health-related information fell to a survey low of 20%. Trust in Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. fell to a survey low of 25%. Trust in congressional Republicans (20%) and Democrats (25%) also were at lows. By the numbers: 43% of Americans said they support the idea of establishing a "Medicare for All" program to provide government-run health insurance to all, largely replacing private health insurance; 24% oppose the idea and 32% say they aren't sure. Nearly half of independents (47%) support it, as do 62% of Democrats. 21% of Republicans support Medicare for All, and 27% are undecided, compared with 52% who oppose the idea. The other side: Opponents said their top reason is they fear Medicare for All would have a worse quality of care than private insurance. Other reasons were feeling it would become too expensive for taxpayers; that government should not be providing health care; or that it would expand the size of government too much. But resistance to the idea has changed markedly from recent campaign cycles,…

33e1d7779a:120fc6b0d7df2e83.title: A golden age of corporate profits
33e1d7779a:120fc6b0d7df2e83.author: Matt Phillips
33e1d7779a:120fc6b0d7df2e83.summary: Data: U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis, FactSet; Chart: Axios/Matt Phillips; Note: After-tax profit data includes inventory and capital depreciation adjustments. Corporate America is raking in record profits, luxuriating in luscious margins and capturing the largest chunk of the country's income on record. Why it matters: The corporate bonanza is bolstering the stock market, but it may also be playing a role in the persistently sour sentiment among the American electorate. The latest: Tuesday is the unofficial start of third-quarter earnings season as JPMorgan Chase, Goldman Sachs and others report results. Zoom in: Wall Street expects the members of the blue-chip S&P 500 index to continue to make it rain. Third-quarter earnings per share are expected to grow roughly 29% for the index, compared with the quarter in 2025, according to estimate data collected by FactSet. That's after a massive 50% annual increase in second-quarter earnings that was supercharged by the giant, non-operating gains on valuations of tech investments reported by Amazon and Alphabet. (Amazon, for example, penciled in its stake in Anthropic as boosting its profit by more than $50 billion.) But even without those enormous gains, the numbers were quite strong, thanks to the AI boom that analysts expect to keep powering giant profits. What they're saying: The market is still all about AI, but the gains are extremely concentrated . "At the stock level, AI infrastructure stocks are expected to drive more than half of S&P 500 EPS growth in Q3," wrote Ben Snider, chief U.S. equity analyst with Goldman Sachs. Snider noted that more than two-thirds of the total growth in S&P 500 earnings for the quarter is expected to come from just 10 stocks. What's more, Micron Technology and Nvidia alone are expected to generate more than one-third of the growth in earnings for the blue chips, Snider wrote. The big picture: Broader measures of U.S. corporate profitability captured by economic — rather than stock…

33e1d7779a:9e473449adbd2028.title: Every major Nvidia customer is now a competitor as Microsoft reveals new Maia chip
33e1d7779a:9e473449adbd2028.author: Ina Fried
33e1d7779a:9e473449adbd2028.summary: The trillion-dollar AI race is moving from software to silicon, as Microsoft's massive bet on its proprietary Maia chips proves Big Tech wants to wean itself off Nvidia's dominance. Why it matters: Microsoft's plan to power its AI products with custom silicon shows how every major Nvidia customer is now a competitor, seeking lower costs, improved performance and more control. The shift is particularly significant for inference — the computing needed to generate AI responses — as more sophisticated AI models and agents drive demand for computing power. Driving the news: Microsoft unveiled Maia 300, its latest custom AI accelerator, saying it will begin deploying the chip in 2027 and it will become the primary inference system for its own products and services. The company says Maia 300 will deliver 40% more AI tokens per megawatt than leading GPU-based systems. It's also designed to minimize unnecessary data movement between chips and memory, a growing bottleneck as AI models become more complex. The big picture: Microsoft's plan is part of a much broader shift, with nearly all major AI players seeking Nvidia alternatives. Google has been developing its own Tensor Processing Units for years, with its latest generation including separate versions optimized for training AI models and running inference. OpenAI is developing its Jalapeño chip with Broadcom, initially focusing on inference workloads. The company said in August that its first chip was outperforming Nvidia hardware on certain workloads and that it was already developing subsequent generations. Amazon has its own ⁠ Trainium family of AI chips, which are being used by customers including Anthropic. OpenAI has also committed to using Amazon's custom silicon as part of a massive infrastructure agreement.
